"I would offer, he would take one or two, that's all." Prabhupāda grinned. "Later on, one dozen!" We all laughed, and he remembered yet more *prasādam* pastimes. "And that boy? Stryadhīśa. He would take at least twenty *capātīs.* 'Stryadhisa, can I offer you?' 'Yes.' I gave four. Again finished, again four."

"You must have been surprised to see how much they could eat," Tamal suggested.

"Hmm, I was not surprised. He was young man, very stout and strong."

Kīrtanānanda said that originally they all ate from Prabhupāda's plate. "There was one plate of *prasādam.* And Prabhupāda would just give little, little to everybody. And everybody would be satisfied."

Prabhupāda confirmed this. "I used to keep some *prasādam*, anyone would come I would give. In meeting, I used to collect not less than six dollars, not more than twenty dollars. And that was three times a week." He added, "They purchased my books. In Butler also, many churches would purchase."

As we walked into Central Park the handiwork of our devotees was in evidence everywhere. A large party of men were out most of last night, plastering the lampposts and street lights with posters advertising Ratha-yātrā. In anticipation of the festival and fully confident of its potential for changing the hearts and minds of the general populace, Śrīla Prabhupāda encouraged the devotees in their efforts. "You convince the authorities of America of my logic, *andha-paṅgu-nyāya*, lame and blind logic. America is blind by money. When one gets too much money, he becomes blind. *Tasmād bhajanti kavayo dhana-durmadāndhāḥ.* To get too much riches means he becomes fool and blind; he doesn't care. So this blindness of America, and we Indians, we have no money, but we have got culture. Combine together, then things will be very nicely done for the good of the whole world. Simply money is not the end; there must be culture. Take that culture, Vedic culture, and use it by American money. Then the whole world will be paradise, Vaikuṇṭha."

\* \* \*

Viśākhā dāsī arranged for another group photo for BTG. It was the most impressive photo yet. The size of the building made it impossible to have everyone stand on the pavement outside, so she made some special arrangements. Prabhupāda came out onto the half-roof on the third floor and sat on his lotus-flower *vyāsāsana*, with his senior men gathered around him. The other devotees waved from every window on all eleven floors, as Viśākhā took her shots from the roof of the building across the road.

\* \* \*

Prabhupāda has refused to either adjust his diet or take the different medicines. He said that the anxieties of managing ISKCON are the cause his pain and that the GBC should learn how to relieve him of it.

\* \* \*

Tamal Krishna Mahārāja came to Prabhupāda with a doubt he had about the work going on in New Vrindaban. He wanted to know whether it was all right that Kīrtanānanda Mahārāja was expending so much money and energy on building the palace. Surely this was at the expense of book distribution he suggested.

Śrīla Prabhupāda assured him it was proper. "No, it is all right. He is doing it as an offering to his guru."

\* \* \*

Ten GBCs are here now, representing both North and South America. They had meetings for most of yesterday and again today. While Śrīla Prabhupāda took his massage they came onto the roof of the building to inform him of their decisions. They have decided to make Puṣṭa Kṛṣṇa Swami the GBC for the West Coast, from Berkeley to points north. He is taking Jagadīśa prabhu's place, who, on the insistence of Śrīla Prabhupāda, is now full-time GBC for education. They appointed Harikeśa Swami as Prabhupāda's new secretary. However Puṣṭa Kṛṣṇa Mahārāja will remain in the post until we leave for England in three days.

The body also confirmed Śrīla Prabhupāda's appointment of Tamal Krishna Mahārāja as GBC for New York and Rādhā-Dāmodara TSKP to replace Madhudviṣa. They added life membership and trusteeship of ISKCON properties to his portfolio.

Prabhupāda is very pleased with Tamal Krishna Mahārāja's organizational skills. Both the temple and Rādhā-Dāmodara TSKPs are quickly clearing away the enormous debts which the previous temple administration incurred, even though this accelerated debt liquidation is preventing money from being sent to India.

Satsvarūpa Goswami and Ghanaśyāma dasa arrived a few days ago with Mahābuddhi prabhu, who has just returned from his highly successful tour of the libraries and universities in India. They met with His Divine Grace several times, presenting him with a written plan to expand the Library Party's activities around the globe. Running out of places to go in America, they proposed going to Europe, Asia and the South Seas. Prabhupāda read their report and approved it, giving them his wholehearted support, even to the point that when Gopāla Kṛṣṇa prabhu phoned from India to insist that Mahābuddhi return, Prabhupāda said no, that he must now do a world tour. Prabhupāda had also suggested that Gurudāsa Swami join them as a classroom lecturer.

However, the GBC, while approving the Library Party members' plans, decided Satsvarūpa Mahārāja was more needed in the USA, and should remain to properly oversee the temples in his jurisdiction.

Śrīla Prabhupāda accepted their decision, even though it overruled his own previous approval. He was happy to see his leading managers cooperatively working together to solve problems and promote the preaching, and he gladly deferred to them.

The GBC men also dealt with one extra item on their agenda: Śrīla Prabhupāda himself. Concerned about his health, they requested him not to travel or give classes, and to rest in New York until his health improves. Śrīla Prabhupāda modestly accepted their concern for him. He tipped his head. "I have no objection."

\* \* \*

Śrīla Prabhupāda answered a couple of letters today from devotees in America. Dāmodara Paṇḍita dāsa from New Vrindaban had several questions. He said he had heard some tape recordings of Śrīla Prabhupāda's Godbrother, Kṛṣṇadāsa Bābājī, singing some devotional songs. He wondered if they were bona fide or not. He also asked if it was a good idea to make a comparative study of different philosophies from the Kṛṣṇa conscious standpoint. He felt it might be useful in our preaching work.

Śrīla Prabhupāda replied that he had not heard the recordings of his Godbrother, so he could not make a judgment of them. Apart from this he said, "You should just go on chanting Hare Krishna Mahamantra and the Pancatattva mantra and don't divert your attention. You cannot understand the meaning of the Indian songs and simply parrot like chanting of these songs has no value."

He told him that comparison of philosophy was a difficult task unless one was expert. Prabhupāda doubted its necessity for general preaching. "First of all, let people understand Krishna. We are doing that. Maybe one or two are interested in philosophy and for so few persons we can't spare so much valuable time. Better to induce everyone to chant Hare Krishna and take prasadam. That will be a mass benevolent activity. In the western countries many Ph.D.'s are out of employment because they do not get any service. We do not want to become great philosophers but rather to understand the philosophy in our own books. If we remain strong in our own literature, we can meet anyone else without any fear."

He ended his letter by telling him that he would visit New Vrindaban again, as soon as the palace is complete. "I very much appreciated how everyone is living peacefully and happily at New Vrindaban."

In a letter from Los Angeles, Dhṛṣṭaketu dāsa, a BBT worker, asked for Śrīla Prabhupāda to clarify his instructions on the growing of hair. Dhṛṣṭaketu had heard it said that Śrīla Prabhupāda did not consider a person with long hair to be his disciple. If this was so, he wanted to know the reason, as there are photos of our previous spiritual masters with hair and beards.

Śrīla Prabhupāda confirmed his dislike for long hair. "Unless absolutely necessary, one should keep head shaven and not allow the hair to grow long. If absolutely necessary, one can dress like an American gentleman, with short hair, but long hair is prohibited. The reason that one with long hair is not my disciple is because he is against the principle. Unless absolutely necessary one should keep hair short, and if necessary one can dress like an American gentleman with short hair. It is not expected that everyone will join. For that reason we can't compromise. The tendency is there to be hippy. When the acaryas are seen with beard, that is during Caturmasya, July-September. If observed strictly there is not simply a beard. There are so many rules and regulations. One can't eat a variety of foods. Only kitri prepared and poured on the floor, and then licked up. There are so many other rules also. That is not always that they kept beard."

In Gopāla Kṛṣṇa prabhu's last letter, and then again during a phone call, he requested Śrīla Prabhupāda to give him a special power of attorney so he could initiate a court case against a Vṛndāvana *bābājī*. Prabhupāda had negotiated to buy land at the back of our temple in December last year with the man. Under the signed agreement the *bābājī* was to sell his land for thirty thousand rupees. He is now demanding four hundred thousand. Although we have already laid a drainage pipe through Mr. Dalmia's property in front of the land, the *bābājī* is now blocking the pipe. The effluence is falling on Mr. Dalmia's land, making him angry, and making it urgently necessary for us to fight the case in court. In his letter Gopāla Kṛṣṇa prabhu said that Bhagatjī feels the local municipal councilor and the local *gosvāmīs* are behind the trouble since the *bābājī* is an old man, without resources to fight us without some kind of backing.

Accordingly, Śrīla Prabhupāda sent out the power of attorney today. He made it out in favor of Akṣayānanda Swami and Haihaya prabhu.

\* \* \*

At 4:30 p.m. Śrīla Prabhupāda held a lengthy interview with the editor of a monthly magazine for expatriate Indians, called *Trans-India*. A perceptive man, the editor asked intelligent questions. He had interviewed a number of devotees yesterday and had a good grasp of how ISKCON worked.

He began with an observation of Śrīla Prabhupāda's uniqueness amongst the preachers of Indian spirituality. "Ever since Vivekananda came here in 1893 there has been a lot of interest in this country in Indian philosophy. Recent gurus have come, they have talked about meditation. My own view is that all of these things have influenced the American people, but in a kind of intellectual fad, a kind of fashion. And it seems to me that your intention and aim is not merely to cater to the mind, cater to reason, cater to the intellect, but to effect a kind of transformation of man himself. Is this why you have introduced a whole way of living, a whole way of life, is it? Am I right in suggesting that?"

Śrīla Prabhupāda gave a lengthy reply, explaining, as he did with Mr. Orwell, that spiritual life was on a different platform of work than the material. He elaborated on the difference of the soul and the body, explaining that he was trying to educate people to the real standard of civilized life, in pursuance of Lord Caitanya's order.

The editor asked Śrīla Prabhupāda the difference between his message and that of other gurus.

Prabhupāda replied, "First of all, we do not accept anyone as guru if he's not competent to understand *Bhagavad-gītā* and preach it also. He's not a guru. The guru's definition given in the *Bhagavad-gītā.* Kṛṣṇa said to Arjuna, 'My dear Arjuna, this *Bhagavad-gītā* philosophy or yoga system, first of all I spoke to the sun-god. And then he spoke to his son, Manu. Then Manu spoke to his son, Ikṣvāku.' In this way the knowledge comes down from the spiritual master to the disciple, or from the father to the son. So unless one comes in this disciplic succession, he cannot become guru. All the swamis and yogis who came here, they do not belong to this *paramparā* system, so therefore they are not bona fide guru. They are presenting themselves as guru, but they are not guru. Therefore people are misled. People are misled, and this is the first time that we presented India's traditional philosophy and life as it is understood by the *paramparā* system. Therefore it is being so well received."

Since the man had begun by mentioning Vivekananda, Prabhupāda used his work as an example of non-*paramparā* ineffectiveness. "Vivekananda came here, as you said, 1893, before my birth. I was born in 1896. But they have worked for, say, eighty-five years. What they have done? But I have worked here for seven or eight years, and it is now world-wide movement. Why? Because we presented the things as they are. Therefore it is effective. So if the things are presented as they are, the customers will automatically come."

When, a little into the conversation, the man asked what Śrīla Prabhupāda's plans were for India, Prabhupāda used the opportunity to enlarge on this principle of being an authorized preacher. At the same time he gave an interesting synopsis of his early efforts to preach. "I wanted to start this Movement from India. I even requested Mahatma Gandhi, that 'Mahatmaji, you have got some respect all over the world, and you are known as a great student of *Bhagavad-gītā.* Now you have got your *svarāj*, the Britishers have gone away. Let us preach *Bhagavad-gītā.*' But I don't think I got any reply from him. Of course he was very busy man. My letter might have reached him or not reached him. The secretaries might have rejected. I think received from secretary, like that. But then after few days he was killed. So I was trying for this purpose in India. I approached many friends, that 'You have got four sons. Give me one son so that I can train him how to become a real preacher of *Bhagavad-gītā* how one can understand.' Because *Bhagavad-gītā* is being misinterpreted. So I wanted to preach it as it is. That was my mission. So practically nobody joined me. Then I decided to come here, and these boys cooperated.

"So I have got great desire to, because India is by nature Kṛṣṇa conscious. But our modern leaders keeping them suppressed, that is the difficulty. There are so many other difficulties, and leaders are misinterpreting *Bhagavad-gītā.* To tell you frankly, there are so many commentaries on *Bhagavad-gītā* by Dr. Radhakrishnan, by Gandhi, by Tilak, by Aurobindo or many others. But nobody has said that 'Here is God, Kṛṣṇa.' Do you admit or not? Has anybody said that, 'Here is God, Kṛṣṇa. You are searching after God. Here is the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Kṛṣṇa. Worship Him'? Nobody has stated. Am I right or not?"

The editor said he hadn't read many different commentaries. Just Gandhi's and Radhakrishnan's.

"Gandhiji has preached or Dr. Radhakrishnan has written," Prabhupāda continued, "but who has preached that Kṛṣṇa is the Supreme Personality of Godhead, He is to be worshiped? Just like we are preaching. Here in America, you have seen our temple. How they are worshiping Kṛṣṇa? So *Bhagavad-gītā*, main purpose is that. Kṛṣṇa says *sarva-dharmān parityajya mām ekaṁ śaraṇaṁ vraja.* So who has preached this? So although they came—so many swamis, yogis and politicians—they came, but they talked—what can I say?—all irrelevant. Nobody spoke that 'Kṛṣṇa is the Supreme Personality of Godhead. You worship Him.' Nobody has said. This is the first time, I am saying. Do you agree or not?"

"Yes. Do you think that this is because of the Western influence under which they have gone?"

"They did not come to teach," Prabhupāda said. "But they wanted to be victimized by the Western people. They had no strength to save themselves. They have no strength. They have no determination. Hodgepodge, that's all. Therefore it was not successful; not a single man became Kṛṣṇa conscious. Even nowadays." Once again he cited Vivekananda. "He is famous in India that 'He preached in America, all Americans have become Vedantists,' something like that. Now, practically, you have gone in Vṛndāvana?"

The editor said he had, but before our temple was opened, so he had not seen it.

"So we have got our temple," Prabhupāda said, "that is considered the best temple in Vṛndāvana. Thousands and thousands of Americans went to Vṛndāvana for our temple and other temples. But there is another Vivekananda, Ramakrishna *āśrama*, nobody went there. Not a single person. So what preaching they have done, from practical point of view? So many men went to our temple. They had no inquiry even that 'We have heard that there is a Ramakrishna Mission Temple here, where it is?' Vṛndāvana is not a very big city, everyone knows. Nobody, not a single person went there. And they visited other temples. So what kind of preaching, hmm? What do you think?"

The editor hypothesized that a religion could not be expected to prosper or even survive in a culture that was the very antithesis of what it stood for. "And that's why your Movement, you are trying to suggest that the only way you can attain *mokṣa*, or liberation, or whatever, is through a particular kind of culture that you are propagating."

Prabhupāda quickly responded that it was not a "particular" culture he was propagating; it was *the* culture. He quoted two verses from *Bhagavad-gītā.* The first, ([4.9](https://vedarama.com/en/books/bg/4.9)) said that if one understands Kṛṣṇa as He is, one never has to take birth again in the material realm; the second, ([9.3](https://vedarama.com/en/books/bg/9.3)), stated that one who has no faith in Kṛṣṇa's teachings cannot escape the repeated cycle of birth and death. "They do not know it, what is cycle of birth and death, how one can get out of it. Just like the flies with great force falls in the fire. They are very busy. What is their busy-ness? Falling in the fire. This is going on. So this Kṛṣṇa consciousness movement is just to save the people who go down by the force of the laws of material nature in the cycle of birth and death."

The editor asked one last question and then took his leave. He seemed very satisfied with his interview and honored to have met Śrīla Prabhupāda.

\* \* \*

Before the *Trans-India* interview, one of the devotees had supplied to Śrīla Prabhupāda a *Time* magazine to give him an idea of what type of magazine *Trans-India* was. After the depature of the interviewer Prabhupāda browsed through the *Time* for a few minutes. Looking up from his desk and pushing the magazine away to its edge he told me, "No one should read these magazines. They are presented in such a way that it makes the material world appear as if it is real."

\* \* \*

In the evening the devotees showed Prabhupāda a film of last week's Philadelphia Ratha-yātrā which Prabhupāda enjoyed.

Tamal Krishna detailed some of the plans for tomorrow's New York Ratha-yātrā. Hundreds of devotees are already here, with many more expected. The parade will begin at 2:00 p.m. and is expected to reach Washington Square Park by 4:00 p.m.

Tamal Krishna Mahārāja wanted to leave it to Śrīla Prabhupāda to decide his degree of participation; however, he made three suggestions: Prabhupāda could come at the start and go the whole way, just come at the end, or join the parade halfway. Tamal said the devotees would be more than happy with whatever Prabhupāda decided; they were already fully satisfied just knowing he was there.

Prabhupāda, however, left it to Tamal to make the decision. So after consultation with other senior leaders, Tamal proposed that Prabhupāda join the carts at about the halfway mark. This would allow Śrīla Prabhupāda to follow his normal schedule of noon massage, bath, lunch and a rest before joining the parade around 3:00 p.m. They felt that would not be too strenuous. He said they had arranged for a Winnebago with a toilet in it to travel along side the chariots in case Śrīla Prabhupāda required it.

Prabhupāda appreciated this thoughtfulness, recalling that when he attended the London Ratha-yātrā three years ago he had walked the whole route, but it was troublesome because of his kidney problems.

## July 18th, 1976

Prabhupāda has been waiting for this day when he can witness Ratha-yātrā in the place he first began ISKCON just ten years ago.

Śrīla Prabhupāda maintained his regular program this morning, except there was no class because all the devotees were fully engaged in preparing for the festival. We drove past the *ratha* site just in time to see the devotees pulling the chariots to the parade start. As we neared them, Śrīla Prabhupāda suggested that the devotees include all the temple vehicles in the procession. "Full opulence," he said as he smiled. "*ṣaḍ-aiśvarya-pūrṇa.*"

Tamal Krishna Mahārāja caught up the proposal with enthusiasm, lamenting that only three buses and a few vans were present out of the twenty-five vans and eight buses the Rādhā-Dāmodara party has. However, he and Ādi-keśava assured Prabhupāda they would at least all be there along with all the temple cars, with the exception of the older vehicles.

Ādi-keśava told us that each chariot weighed fourteen thousand pounds. Even with their top canopies lowered they looked formidable. Seven and a half feet tall steel wheels were covered in mirrors, and their brightly painted frames dazzled. Prabhupāda was very impressed with them, commenting several times how strong and nicely made they were. Jayānanda prabhu, who Rāmeśvara Mahārāja said had worked throughout the last five nights to ensure the carts were ready, was leading the carts looking tired, yet blissful. He had been working all night with sixty other men to get the carts to the beginning of the parade route, and had drafted another fifteen men to help with one of the chariots that was refusing to budge.

Just as Śrīla Prabhupāda's car pulled close, that chariot began to move. The devotees were all shouting, "Prabhupāda! Balarāma!" to gain both strength and enthusiasm. When they saw Śrīla Prabhupāda in the car they began to shout and pull with even greater vigor. "*Jaya* Prabhupāda!" they called out. Śrīla Prabhupāda smiled and called back, "*Jaya.* Hare Kṛṣṇa!"

Rāmeśvara reminded Śrīla Prabhupāda how in the *Caitanya-caritāmṛta* he had written that just as the cart of Jagannātha in Puri is compared to Mount Sumeru, similarly, in London they were comparing it to Lord Nelson's column.

Prabhupāda said the British newspaper, the *Guardian*, had published its report with the words, "Rival to Nelson's column."

Tamal Krishna said the *Guardian* was a good newspaper. Prabhupāda, however, felt they were now against us for political reasons. "Only politics. So mean-minded, they have no idea even beyond politics."

As we walked around the park Tamal Krishna Mahārāja told Śrīla Prabhupāda that when they had applied to the city for permission to hold Ratha-yātrā they only said it was going to be a small parade with some hand-drawn floats. Tamal laughed. "Another trick of the Hare Kṛṣṇas."

Prabhupāda smilingly compared them to Lord Vāmana asking Bali Mahārāja for charity. "Bali Mahārāja was asked for three feet of land. 'Very good. You speak so nicely, such intelligent, but You are boy; You do not know how to ask. I can give You a big island.' 'No, I must be satisfied as I require. I don't want more. Only three feet, that's all.'"

Prabhupāda told us that right now he was writing about that story in the Eighth Canto of *Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam*. He described how Bali Mahārāja's guru, ‚ukrācārya, had chastised his disciple, "'Rascal, if you give like that, where you will stay? He'll take everything!' *Smārta-brāhmaṇa.* Simply considering, 'How I shall live?' He rejected guru. 'You are not guru.'"

Satsvarūpa Mahārāja asked, "But that guru told him to worship Viṣṇu officially."

"No," Prabhupāda said. "He was by nature Vaiṣṇava, like the grandfather, Prahlāda Mahārāja."

Satsvarūpa Mahārāja said that although Bali was born in a demon family, he was not a demon. Śrīla Prabhupāda confirmed that, adding another one of his interesting observations. "Demon family, still, they are *kṣatriyas.* Just like the Europeans and Americans, they were *kṣatriyas*, now they have become demons. Actually they are *kṣatriyas.* I have studied. And the Jews are *vaiśyas."*

That brought a laugh, since Rāmeśvara and Tamal Krishna are both from Jewish families.Tamal Krishna added humorously, "That's why they call them the American Maḍwaris."

Prabhupāda laughed. "Yes. They know how to do business and earn money."

Rāmeśvara Mahārāja noted the day's clear sky, prompting Prabhupāda to produce another humorous anecdote. "Yes, good morning. When the sky is clear the Englishmen call, 'Good morning.' This is the origin of 'good morning,' because, unfortunately, in their country the sky is never clear. If by chance some day it is clear, they say, 'Oh, it is a good morning.' That is the origin of that. One Englishman told me."

"But now they always greet each other by saying 'Good morning, sir,'" Tamal said.

"No, it has become now a phrase. But originally the word originated when the morning was good, because that is a great fortune for them. Yes, in London I was three months; always gloomy, damp, cloudy. Therefore on television they asked, 'What is your idea of hell?' and I, 'This is hell, London.' He stopped; he did not ask anything more. This is hell. Simply by big, big buildings, you are keeping as heaven, but it is the hell." Everyone laughed.

Having spent a lot of time in India with Śrīla Prabhupāda, Tamal Krishna Mahārāja knew Prabhupāda's view of the history of the British Raj. "The British propagated in India though that everything was like milk and honey in Britain."

Prabhupāda smiled. "They propagated the Thames River as very big river. And when I first saw it—it is canal."

Our route back to the car took us past the Museum of Natural History. Rāmeśvara said that the planetarium presented atheistic arguments to show life as being chemically based with the stars created by chemical reactions.

Tamal Krishna said that as a child he had gone and played with an exhibit of a number of weighing scales which each purported to give the weight of a person on a particular planet. The scale for the moon planet showed his weight to be one-sixth his weight on earth. He asked Śrīla Prabhupāda if the idea of lighter weight was correct.

"First thing is that it is full of life. Full of very, very intelligent demigods," Prabhupāda replied. "They have never gone."

"If a devotee were to go to the moon, would he see all of these very intelligent demigods?" Tamal asked.

"Yes."

"So if someone actually went there, they would see this life. It's not that you have to have special vision to see it."

"But you have to qualify yourself," Prabhupāda added.

\* \* \*

Prabhupāda took his massage, *prasādam* and rest half an hour earlier than usual, so he was ready to go when the car arrived at 3:00 p.m. to take him to the parade. As the car moved down 7th Avenue across the intersections we could see the chariots making their way down 5th Avenue. The parade was so long that the lead cart, Lord Jagannātha's, and the third one, Lord Balarāma's, crossed two different junctions simultaneously, both surrounded by huge crowds of devotees and onlookers.

Our car pulled up at the Empire State Building, on 34th Street and 5th Avenue, where Prabhupāda waited the arrival of the chariots. We looked back up 5th Avenue to see the incredible spectacle of three brightly festooned *rathas*, their multicolored canopies reaching high into the air, majestically gliding down the man-made concrete canyon with an entourage stretching back for blocks. Six hundred devotees chanted and danced in multiple *kīrtana* parties, in front and on all sides, glorifying the Lord of the universe. Many thousands of onlookers lined the sidewalks, including a large turnout from the Indian community. Prabhupāda said it was a long-cherished dream come true.

The lead chariot went past us and then the parade came to a halt. Śrīla Prabhupāda stepped out of his car and, surrounded by an escort of *sannyāsīs* using their *daṇḍas* as a makeshift barrier, he approached Lady Subhadrā's chariot, his hands held together in respectful *praṇāmas.* Prabhupāda walked slowly through the crowd which pressed forward to see him, almost hemming him in. Television and news reporters were there in force. They were practically fighting with each other to try to get their photo shots and a possible interview. Śrīla Prabhupāda ascended the chariot and sat comfortably on the *vyāsāsana* which the devotees had mounted under the front deck between the wheels.

With Tamal Krishna Mahārāja, Kīrtanānanda Mahārāja, Rādhāballabha dāsa, Candanācārya dāsa, myself and some other devotees flanking him, the parade restarted. Rādhāballabha carried a walkie-talkie. He told me afterward that he and several others who stuck close by Śrīla Prabhupāda throughout the parade were all armed in case there was any trouble. But everything went very smoothly—ecstatically—as one large group of devotees after another took turns to come before Subhadrā's chariot, each one chanting and dancing with abandon before His Divine Grace before peeling off to make way for the next. And all along the route New Yorkers and tourists stood by the roadside, amazed and delighted by the grand spectacle.

After an hour or so the chariots arrived at their Washington Square Park destination where many thousands more spectators were milling around, inspecting various booths and awaiting the arrival of the Lord. Our chariot pulled into the park, just at the side of a large stage. Prabhupāda, grinning broadly, dismounted and was led to the stage while the devotees prepared for his lecture.

The smoothness with which the devotees had handled the parade was marred somewhat at this point because they made the mistake of thinking that they could use the *vyāsāsana* from the chariot for Śrīla Prabhupāda's lecture on stage. But they had problems getting it moved, and this resulted in Prabhupāda having to stand around for about ten minutes while they struggled to set it up. He asked for water, but none was on hand, and it was another fifteen minutes before some arrived. Prabhupāda became a little annoyed with all this. Then devotees proceeded to bring the three deities to a platform directly behind and above him during his lecture, thus interrupting him. But apart from these hitches, Prabhupāda was delighted with the whole affair. It was an impressive achievement in the most famous and important city in the world, and a triumphant climax to Prabhupāda's American tour.

His talk was very short. He began by giving a brief summary of the origin of the festival, describing how Kṛṣṇa came to take the form of Lord Jagannātha. "Formerly one king of the name Indradyumna, he started the temple of Jagannātha in Orissa at Purī. Perhaps some of you have gone there, know there is a very, very old temple, according to modern calculation, not less than two thousand years old. There is the Jagannātha Deity. The King was very much anxious to establish a temple of Kṛṣṇa, Balarāma and Subhadrā, but there was a contract between the sculptor and the King that the sculptor would go on working in closed door and the King should not disturb him. But when many days passed the King felt, 'What this worker is doing?' So he forcefully opened the door, and he saw that the sculptor could not finish the Deity. So this form of Jagannātha, Kṛṣṇa, Balarāma and Subhadrā was unfinished. They were going under construction, carving, but the King forcibly opened the door. Therefore the King said, 'I shall worship this unfinished Deity, never mind.' So this Jagannātha you see in this form because King Indradyumna wanted to worship Him in that form. So this is devotee's willing; Kṛṣṇa accepts everyone's devotional service if it is offered with love and affection."

He said anyone from anywhere in the world could worship Kṛṣṇa because He is the father of all living entities, as described in the *Bhagavad-gītā.* "*Sarva-yoniṣu kaunteya mūrtayaḥ sambhavanti yāḥ/ tāsāṁ brahma mahad yonir ahaṁ bīja-pradaḥ pitā.* God is the supreme father of everyone. If we simply study this verse, that the mother nature is the mother of all living entities, and God is the supreme father of everyone, we can study these two lines very carefully. On the earth we can see so many living entities are coming out, beginning from the grass, then so many insects, reptiles, big trees, then animals, birds, beasts, then human beings, they are all coming from the earth, and they are living at the expense of earth. The earth is supplying food to everyone. As the mother gives life or maintains the child by the milk of her breast, similarly, the earth mother is maintaining all different types of living entities. There are different forms of life, and Mother Earth is supplying food.

"We see the mother, Mother Earth, and we see the children in different forms, then we must accept that there is father, because without father there is no possibility of mother begetting children. You simply understand this philosophy of father, mother and children, then you can very easily understand that there is God, the supreme father; there is no difficulty. But if you do not become reasonable as human being, if you remain as animal like cats and dogs, the dogs cannot understand that there is the supreme father, God, but a human being can understand. He has got intelligence. So with this advanced intelligence, if we do not understand about the existence of God, our relationship with Him, and what is our duty in that relationship, then this human form of life will be spoiled. Our, this Kṛṣṇa consciousness movement is checking the human society from spoiling the human form of life. This human form of life, by the evolutionary process we have got after millions and millions of years, and if we spoil this life eating, sleeping, mating and defending like the cats and dog without any sense of God, then our life is spoiled. So please do not take this Kṛṣṇa consciousness movement as any sectarian movement. It is the science of God."

He ended, "We have got so many books. So kindly take advantage of this Movement and impartially try to understand what is the purpose of this Movement, why we are distributing so many literatures. Soberly and with calm head, try to understand this Movement and be happy. That is our only mission. Thank you very much."

To the cheers of the huge crowd of devotees, Śrīla Prabhupāda dismounted the stage and returned to the temple, leaving his disciples to continue on with the festival into the late evening.

Once back at the temple he immediately took rest, even though it was only 6:30 in the evening. He was strained, but happy. As I massaged his legs he lay back and laughed, "I thought there would be some fanaticism!" He was referring to a heckler who stood on the square's fountain at the back of the crowd shouting protests during his lecture. "Did you see that man?" he asked me. "One large black man came up and *Thump*! he knocked him in the water." Prabhupāda had seen it all from the stage and he chuckled as he recalled the incident.

Actually there was practically no disturbance from anyone, except a few fanatic Christians who marched alongside the parade carrying placards that read "Turn or Burn."

\* \* \*

Prabhupāda got up again at 8:00 and Tamal Krishna Mahārāja and Bali-mardana prabhu came to give detailed reports on the day's events. According to them the festival was a great and unqualified success. There were no real incidents to speak of, and even the police were very happy. Sudāmā Mahārāja and his troupe enthralled the crowd with their dramas. The devotees sold books, made life members, and ran various preaching booths. Devotees came from almost every temple in America and Canada and from as far away as South America to make it a truly international celebration. Everyone agreed that it was the biggest and most successful festival ISKCON has staged in the West. Tamal Krishna Mahārāja estimated that between thirty and forty thousand people went through the park in five or six hours. Over seven thousand people enjoyed seven different kinds of free *prasādam*, and sales of sweets and watermelon slices brought in over five thousand dollars.

Prabhupāda liked it when they told him a single piece of *burfī* sold for a dollar and that a slice of melon went for fifty cents. "People, they are simple here. They are not, about money matters, so much attracted. They have got enough money. They don't care. They want that it is good taste, that's all."

Typically, Prabhupāda asked if the crazy boy who had been shouting also got *prasādam.* Tamal told him he thought he must have because free *prasādam* was given to everyone.

Prabhupāda also asked if the police were given *prasādam.* Tamal said he wasn't sure because Toṣaṇa Kṛṣṇa prabhu was looking after them. "We'll bring them some present tomorrow," he said. "But they made the statement that 'If every parade was so beautiful and so nicely orderly, we would be very happy.'"

"Yes," Prabhupāda said. "And that cannot be expected from any other group, only in this group. Such a huge crowd, and there was not a single instance of violence."

Prabhupāda suggested to them that the devotees purchase a building in the Washington Square locale and have two parades: one going and, seven days later, another returning. Lord Jagannātha could stay in the downtown building and a weeklong festival could be held in the park. Then the rest of the year they could use the house for preaching. He had previously told them they could open temples in every district of New York. "Uptown, downtown, all around the town!"

Tamal Krishna attempted to persuade Prabhupāda to remain in New York, tempting him with the temple facilities and the promise of being able to write. He said that if Prabhupāda came to stay he and the devotees would work day and night and give up all personal considerations in order to preach.

Prabhupāda laughed at his persistence, praising his determination. He said that he was agreeable to the offer, but other devotees wanted to see him too. Apart from that, he said that in India his presence was required. "If the government is going against our Movement, then I'll have to stay. There is no alternative." Prabhupāda told us that as a result of the Emergency called by Indira Gandhi, and the jailing of her opponents, the result will be that she and her Congress Party will never be elected again. "That is sure. Therefore she's postponing election. Now they have lost all their credit. They will never be elected. Congress Party and Indira Gandhi finished."

As we talked ‚ravaṇānanda prabhu came in with some 7 UP. Prabhupāda had asked me for some when he woke from his rest. He sipped the fizzy soft drink and told us, "From my childhood I liked this lemonade. I think it was cost, in our childhood, three *paisā.*"

Puṣṭa Kṛṣṇa Mahārāja came in, exuberant from a full day's chanting and preaching. He had led one of the *kīrtana* groups in the parade. Several times he came before Śrīla Prabhupāda's chariot, his face aglow, fully enlivened to be out with the devotees in the midst of the action. Śrīla Prabhupāda smiled and complimented him, "Puṣṭa Kṛṣṇa Mahārāja chanted."

Puṣṭa Kṛṣṇa also had good things to say about the festival. "Prabhupāda, this festival was wonderful. So many people took *prasādam*, and afterward they had a play and then they did some *bhajanas*, and the people were enchanted by the whole thing. And the neighbors there, they said that 'In the five years I've lived by the park, the park has never been so nice.'"

Prabhupāda inquired whether Ambarīṣa had been there. Bali-mardana said he was in the parade, but had returned to Boston immediately after. He said he had been very willing to cooperate with any publicity and had no objection to his name being used.

It was very late, after ten, and Prabhupāda told the devotees to take rest. "You have all worked so hard."

## July 19th, 1976

The devotees were in Prabhupāda's room early this morning to show him the newspaper coverage of the parade. It was all favorable, and he was especially pleased with the *New York Times* and *Daily News* articles. The *Daily News* had dedicated its center photographic section to the event with many good photos and captions. The headline was "Fifth Avenue, Where East Meets West." The *Times* carried a similar heading, "East Meets West in Hare Krishna Fete."

Śrīla Prabhupāda ordered his secretary to send copies of the papers to Ramkrishna Bajaj. He said that someone other than us should send them to Indira Gandhi. He felt the headlines of the articles had captured what he said yesterday on his walk before the parade. "This title is very nice. This is the point. East, as I say always, the lame man meets the blind man. Together they do wonderful, and different they cannot do anything. He is blind, he is lame. But they join together, Indian culture and American money, they will save the whole world."

Prabhupāda listened as Tamal Krishna Mahārāja read out the *Daily News* article. "Very nicely written. 'With everybody pulling together and everybody puffing together, a huge float is tugged down Fifth Avenue yesterday during the first Ratha-yatra Parade of International Society for Krishna Consciousness. The parade moved south from Central Park to Washington Square Park, where a free feast, music, art, dance and theater festival was held. According to a spokesperson, Ratha-yatra is a time when people come to dance, sing and feast amidst a sublime atmosphere of bright flags, festoons, banners, garlands, flowers and incense, simply to feel the poetry and blissful nature of life.'"

Prabhupāda liked the writing. "Very good, this is blissful nature."

Then Tamal Krishna read out the *New York Times* version of events. "This one is not bad, but it's not so accurate. 'In size it was dwarfed by "Operation Sale." In popular concern it was outweighed by the Democratic National Convention. But for hundreds of Hare Krishna followers, including many Indian immigrants to New York, yesterday's Ratha-yatra festival was by far the most important event in an eventful month. Pulling three brightly-colored chariots down Fifth Avenue from Central Park to Washington Square, the religious group's adherents were celebrating one of the oldest holy days of the Indian calendar, the feast of Jagannatha, the Lord of the Universe, according to Krishna doctrine. Most of the participants in the parade were young Westerners, followers from as far away as Caracas and Montreal. But the crowd included hundreds of Indians who brought the basic Krishna faith with them from Bombay and Calcutta.'"

Prabhupāda felt it good that they had mentioned the Indians. "That's nice."

Tamal Krishna read on. "'Like many other immigrant groups who preserved their forms of worship once they came to America, the Indians who watched or participated in the parade were pleased to see that they could keep the faith even in New York City.'"

Prabhupāda laughed when heard that. "These rascals, let them come, they become *baṛa sāhib.*"

Tamal continued reading. "'While Hare Krishna propounds doctrines of world renunciation common to other varieties of the Hindu faith, the sect, officially known as the International Society for Krishna Consciousness, was founded in 1966 by A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, whose fame as a guru came only after he arrived in the United States in the same year. For most of the Indians watching the parade, however, Hare Krishna was close enough to their brand of Hinduism to make them feel at home.'"

At this Gurudāsa Mahārāja commented that the paper was not taking us lightly by recognizing that we are not a cult. Prabhupāda nodded.

The paper quoted comments from onlookers, Indians, and Westerners, practically all very favorable. "'It's surprising that you find this right in New York City. It's our way of life,' said Nagan Patel, a civil engineer from Jersey City, who immigrated from Bombay. 'We love New York City and America. It's the most beautiful place in the world. No other country will give such freedom for our own ceremony.'"

"That's a fact," Prabhupāda interjected. "That I say always."

Tamal read the last section. "'But the Krishna people were not entirely free of harassment. Along the parade route three men, including one who said he was an Evangelical Christian minister, jeered at the parade and called on parade watchers to become Christians. "Idol worship. This is absolutely ridiculous. Read the Bible," cried one man who would identify himself only as a normal Christian. There was a brief scuffle when an Indian immigrant tried to tear a large placard out of the hands of another heckler. The placard read "Turn or Burn." The police broke things up but made no arrests. "They are insulting us," said the Krishna follower who declined to identify himself. "I'm a devotee of Krishna and Christ. These people who are doing this in the name of Christ are criminals." Except for the hecklers, however, the parade was generally very well received by passersby, who enjoyed the three multi-hued floats, the sun, and the chanting and dancing of the young Krishna marchers. "I think it's great," said Tyrone Adams of Philadelphia, who was paying a visit to his home town of Inglewood, New Jersey. "I'm not religious, but they're all happy and dancing, and that is what life is all about." In Washington Square a crowd of about three thousand, many of whom were there as part of the normal Sunday afternoon activities, heard Swami Prabhupāda deliver a lecture. Later the crowd was served a free vegetarian feast. Along the side, Krishna followers sold Indian sweets, Krishna scriptures, and what one speaker described as 'transcendental paraphernalia.'"

Dhṛṣṭadyumna added that every major television channel carried the story on their news programs last night, with CBS giving it two and half minutes, all of it favorable.

Tamal paraphrased the official in charge of the park who was interviewed by CBS. "He said that, 'We are very proud to be able to say that this park was founded hundreds of years ago, when America was religious.' And he said, 'Spiritual life is still present in Washington Square Park.'"

Śrīla Prabhupāda was very pleased with the reportage. On the walk today Prabhupāda again suggested they have a second festival, one week after the first, which is called Ultā-ratha. He said the deities could stay downtown for a week and then return in a similar procession to their permanent home.

\* \* \*

Śrīla Prabhupāda gave class on *Caitanya-caritāmṛta Madhya-līlā* [20.111](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-madhya/20.111). The verse stated that Lord Kṛṣṇa has three main energies, the spiritual potency, the living entities and the material energy. Using the example of the sun and the sunshine, Prabhupāda described these three emanations of God. He urged his followers to go forward on the basis of real knowledge, and develop their appreciation and relationship with Kṛṣṇa. "You have to study *śāstras* for understanding His position, and if we understand Kṛṣṇa, then we become liberated person immediately. So those who are in Kṛṣṇa consciousness movement, they should study scientifically. Not by sentiment. After full knowledge of Kṛṣṇa, when you become absorbed in Kṛṣṇa's form, that is called *budhā bhāva-samanvitāḥ.* So that *bhāva* stage does not come immediately. You have to practice. There are stages. So, this is the beginning. *Ādau śraddhā.* Just like yesterday. They very much appreciated this Ratha-yātrā ceremony and they wrote very frankly, 'Here is the point of meeting.' The newspapers they have written like that. It is actually the fact."

New York is the seat of the United Nations, an organization which Śrīla Prabhupāda has often compared ISKCON to, at least in terms of practical effect. The devotees laughed as he said, "We cannot become united nations of united dogs. Everyone is barking. If you practice to bark, then simply some different types of dog, some bulldogs, some greyhounds, so how they will be united? That is not possible. Here is unity. Actually if we take Kṛṣṇa consciousness movement very seriously, scientifically, then there is unity. *Paṇḍita* means learned, he is *sama-darśinaḥ. Brahma-bhūtaḥ prasannātmā na śocati na kā"kṣati /samaḥ sarveṣu bhūteṣu mad-bhaktiṁ labhate parām* \[Bg. [18.54](https://vedarama.com/en/books/bg/18.54)\]. Actually this is the platform where we can unite. And by practical example you have shown everyone dancing and chanting, never mind whether Indian, American, black, white, children or old like me. This is wanted.

"When we thoroughly understand what is the basic principle of Kṛṣṇa consciousness and we understand Vāsudeva, Kṛṣṇa, is the central point, then our life is successful. *Vāsudevaḥ sarvam iti sa mahātmā su-durlabhaḥ. Mahātmā* means 'great soul.' So great soul, one who has understood that Kṛṣṇa is the source of everything. Just like the sun is the source of material energy.

"I request you that each and every one of you just become *mahātmā*, not crippled, but broad-minded. That is possible when we understand Kṛṣṇa is the source of all energy. Thank you very much."

After handing out cookies Śrīla Prabhupāda stepped down from his *vyāsāsana* and returned to his room. Because of his weak health he didn't remain for the initiation ceremony which followed. Gurudāsa Mahārāja conducted the fire ceremony. Jagadīśa prabhu handed out the beads, which had been chanted on by the *sannyāsīs*, along with the new spiritual names to about a hundred candidates. It was one of the biggest initiations of this tour. Among the initiates were Bob Cohen and his wife. Bob had several sessions with Śrīla Prabhupāda in India in 1974, where he was stationed as a Peace Corps worker. Their conversations are now being transcribed into a book to be called *Perfect Questions*, *Perfect Answers.* This morning he received the name Brahmatīrtha dāsa, and his wife is now Bhakti dāsī.

\* \* \*

A letter came from the former wife of a leading *sannyāsī*, pleading that she be allowed to remarry. It was respectfully phrased, explaining her difficulty in being without a husband. She said that she had married at an early age and then one year later her husband took *sannyāsā* when she was eighteen. She explained that somehow she had managed to maintain her Kṛṣṇa consciousness over the last four years, but she felt by her nature she must be married. She did not want anything untoward to happen which would disturb Śrīla Prabhupāda, so she humbly requested him to sanction this. Her current engagement was caring for the temple Deities, where she worked alongside an unmarried *brahmacārī*. Finding some compatibility between the two of them, she requested Śrīla Prabhupāda's blessings to marry him. The *brahmacārī* also signed her letter.

As soon as Prabhupāda heard it he became alarmed. "This is illicit sex!" he said emphatically and called for Tamal Krishna Goswami. Allowing such an action, he felt, would greatly disturb her former husband, who is actively preaching with great success. At the same time he was sympathetic to the girl's honesty in expressing her plight. After some discussion he called for Pālikā dāsī, a friend to the girl, and he requested Pālikā to contact her tell her confidently that "Prabhupāda does not at all approve." He also sent a reply to the girl advising her to leave her present situation and come to New York, where there was opportunity to preach and develop her Kṛṣṇa consciousness in association with other women devotees.

Upendra sent a letter from Fiji giving a vague report on recent events there. He said that after Śrīla Prabhupāda's last letter to Vāsudeva dāsa, he and Vāsudeva had a full day's meeting, which was heated at times. Without giving any details Upendra said that Vāsudeva had already sent what he described as "a very poor summary of the situation." He felt one of the problems was Vāsudeva's conditioning, which makes him think like an Indian, and his own, which makes him think like a Westerner. So somehow or other, it seems they are not agreeing.

Śrīla Prabhupāda has not received anything so far from Vāsudeva in reply to his letter, so he asked Upendra to see that it is sent on to him in Paris.

Śrīla Prabhupāda also dictated several letters connected to the Ratha-yātrā. He sent Jayānanda prabhu a special message of thanks for all his hard work. "My dear Jayananda dasa, Please accept my blessings. For so long I have wanted to have Rathayatra in New York and now at long last you have helped me fulfill this long-cherished dream. The Ratha-carts were very strong and attractive and I thank you and all of your assistants for working so hard to prepare such nice carts. May Krishna bless you all for your sincere service that you may all go on making more and more advancement in Krishna Consciousness."

He also sent similar thank you notes to Toṣaṇa Kṛṣṇa prabhu and Ādi-keśava Mahārāja for all their hard work in organizing the event.

To Mr. Ramakrishna Bajaj Prabhupāda wrote, "Enclosed please find newsclippings of our Rathayatra Festival held on 5th. Avenue, New York last Sunday. They are taking it seriously now, 'East meets West. . .' This is the real platform of United Nations, spiritual understanding. I wish that the coordinator of the Gita Pratisthan will preach the gospel of the Gita on this understanding."

And to Jayapatāka Swami in Māyāpur he sent a similar batch of clippings, with a request that he give copies to Mr. Chaudhuri, the man who visited him in February from the Department of Development and Planning in Calcutta. In his own hand he added, "I always remember Mr. Chaudhry and his good wife." He also informed Jayapatāka Mahārāja that Gurukṛpa Swami would be sending him $10,000 per month for construction purposes in Māyāpur.

\* \* \*

Kīrtanānanda Swami came with a box full of clay. He requested Prabhupāda to stand in it so that they could get imprints of his lotus feet. Prabhupāda willingly complied. As he stood on the talcum powder-covered clay surface I pressed on his feet to help make the indent. He stepped off, but the impression was too faint because the clay had filled the whole box and so had nowhere to expand to.

Kīrtanānanda took the box away and returned a few minutes later having removed a one inch strip all the way around. Prabhupāda stepped on again and allowed me to push down on his feet quite firmly. The clay yielded and clear, deep impressions formed, showing even the lines marking the soles of his feet. Everyone was happy with the result. Kīrtanānanda intends to make a mold which will be reproduced in silver for installation in all our temples.

\* \* \*

Prabhupāda had a peaceful evening to himself. At about eight o'clock he went up on the roof and sat silently for a while, accompanied by only myself. He chanted *japa* quietly for about an hour and then returned to his room.

## July 20th, 1976

Instead of walking in Central Park, Prabhupāda took his exercise in Riverside Park, along the Hudson River. He told us this was the route he used to take in 1966 to get to Dr. Misra's apartment in order to do his cooking.

Pointing with his cane to the concrete path, he indicated grass growing here and there. Then he asked why they say that there is no life on the moon. "Life is everywhere, even from the stone it is coming." He explained how scientists say that there is simply sand on the moon, but sand is produced from water. Therefore there must have been water on the moon prior to sand, and thus there must also have been vegetation. According to the *Bhāgavatam* there *is* life on the moon, and Prabhupāda backed up this information with his unerring common sense.

Now with a new group of senior men surrounding him, Prabhupāda again raised the Mars issue, questioning what was the use of going. "What is their idea?"

Atreya Ṛṣi said, "They constantly want to discover more and more so that they can claim that they are lords."

"But what is that discovery?" Prabhupāda asked. "You simply go and see? That's all?"

Atreya could see the pointlessness of it and said there was no really valid purpose.

Rādhāballabha said that it was considered advancement of knowledge.

When Gurudāsa said "They want to colonize because there is overpopulation on this planet," Prabhupāda mocked him. "Eh? Another rascal!"

Gurudāsa grinned and said, "They want to put the American flag on the moon and say, 'It is ours.'"

Prabhupāda struck at the nationalistic mentality with biting humor and sarcasm. "And then lick up. 'Here is American flag.' And then like dog, lick up urine!" His graphic comparison had everyone in stitches. "So lick up, then dog lick urine. It is useless. Dog's business."

When we stopped laughing, Puṣṭa Kṛṣṇa said a little more seriously, "Śrīla Prabhupāda, they feel they should explore the unknown."

"That will remain everlastingly unknown," Prabhupāda said. "They'll never be able to push. Even with the speed of mind and air they go many, many millions of years, it will still be. This verse of *Brahma-saṁhitā*, *panthās tu koṭi-śata-vatsara-sampragamyo vāyor athāpi manaso muni-puṅgavānām/ so' py asti yat-prapada-sīmny avicintya-tattve.* It is inconceivable. It will never be done. They have some vague idea, 'There is no life. There is this. There is that.' Real knowledge they'll never get. Real knowledge you'll get from *Bhāgavata.*"

As we walked along the riverside, with the early morning traffic steadily increasing, Prabhupāda asked what the scientists say about the sun.

Tripurāri Mahārāja replied, "They think it's too hot for life to exist there."

"So how Kṛṣṇa was there?" Prabhupāda asked.

"They don't believe that," Rādhāballabha said.

"So how can I believe you?" Prabhupāda returned. "If you don't believe Kṛṣṇa, shall I have to believe you?"

Rādhāballabha offered the scientific explanation. "They have calculated that as you come within a certain amount, a billion miles of the sun ..."

Prabhupāda showed the flaw in his reasoning. "That is you. That is you, not Kṛṣṇa. That is the difference between you and Kṛṣṇa."

Pursuing the theme of credibility and belief, Rādhāballabha, who is full of little anecdotes denoting the foolishness of almost everyone, told Prabhupāda a short story. "About thirty or forty years ago a man named Orson Welles had a radio show, and just as a joke he started giving a news report that the Martians had landed, and people were panicking. They were trying to leave the city in cars in huge numbers."

Prabhupāda said that was the difference between the less intelligent class, and those with intelligence, the *brāhmaṇas.* "A *śūdra* can be misled at any moment. *Strī-śūdra.* Woman and *śūdra* on the same class." As an example, he told us a story from when he lived in Allahabad. "You can mislead them by high talkings: 'Oh, I am coming from Indian prince.' They come here, marry some European, and go to India and then engage her for collecting water in bucket. One Muhammadan crewman, a vagabond, he bluffed one girl that 'I am coming from Muhammadan prince family.' Then she married, and she went to Allahabad, and she was given *borkhā* and she was living in a hut, and then she was bringing water from the street. She wrote a letter to the Viceroy that 'This is my position.' Then police came and rescued her and sent her home."

Speaking on the gullibility of women made Prabhupāda reflect on the letter he had received yesterday from the *sannyāsī's* widow and the danger of having unprotected women freely mixing with men. Without being prompted he told his managers, "Now there should be one rule that unless they are husband-wife, man and woman should not worship together."

"On the altar?" Puṣṭa Kṛṣṇa asked.

"Yes. Strictly prohibited," Prabhupāda emphasized.

Tamal Krishna asked if that meant on the same altar. He wondered if it was all right if they worked on different altars.

Prabhupāda said no, even if they worked in different sections of the Deity room it should not be allowed. More specifically he stated, "Man and woman together should not worship unless they are husband and wife."

Tamal Krishna Mahārāja wanted to get it very clear. "Never be alone. So just because they are married to someone else, that is not ... They must be married to each other."

Prabhupāda confirmed that his understanding was correct. "They must be together, the man and the woman. The husband-wife can go, not others."

As a longtime GBC Tamal Krishna Mahārāja knew the situation in the temples. "In most temples that is not the system right now."

"No, that system should be introduced," Prabhupāda said. "The husband-wife together can go to worship the Deity. If they are not related as husband, they should not go."

Puṣṭa Kṛṣṇa Swami thought of another possible scenario. "What about a situation like this, where the husband and wife are worshiping, but also some other *brahmacārīs* are also worshiping?"

"Still, that is some protection," Prabhupāda told his GBCs. "The husband is there. The woman means her husband must be there."

By this time the traffic was quite busy, building up for the rush hour. We got into the car and on the way back Rāmeśvara and Tamal Krishna told Prabhupāda they had been to the Museum of Natural History the day before. Tamal said he got a headache after three hours.

Prabhupāda sympathized with him. "From seeing the dead bodies." Then he smiled.

Rāmeśvara told him about the displays. "They have this one trying to prove the Darwin theory of evolution. They have these bones, and they say this proves how man was formerly like an ape or a monkey. Now he has become more civilized."

Śrīla Prabhupāda's sharp intelligence dissected the logic behind the skeletal show. "So where is Darwin's bones? Darwin got all this knowledge. His bones should be studied first, how he got so much knowledge, and from which monkey he came. By studying the bones, discover it."

Tamal Krishna agreed, "Complete concoction."

Prabhupāda repeated his challenge. "Ask them to find out from which monkey the Darwin's bone has come. They may decide. Study the bones of Darwin." As a final indictment, he added, "And spoiling public money in this way."

Rāmeśvara told him about another display which was much more gruesome than dead bones. "One display showed the different stages of the embryo growing. So to have this display they used actual dead aborted babies. They have them mounted in the display case, the dead babies that they have killed. They have taken their tiny little bodies and put them in a display, so you can see the baby at two months, at four months, at six months, at eight months. Like that."

Prabhupāda didn't betray any shock. Instead he chose to examine the philosophy behind such a grotesque show. "How it is growing? When it was put into the bottle, why it did not grow? It remained as it is."

"They say because they severed its connection with the mother," Rāmeśvara answered matter-of-factly.

"That means the baby has grown from the mother," Prabhupāda said. "So mother is life. That is the proof. Otherwise how the baby has grown? You cannot say that life can be grown out of matter."

"Life from life," Rāmeśvara said.

"That's it," Prabhupāda said.

"No one thinks like that," Rāmeśvara observed.

"They are all rascals," Prabhupāda said. "Therefore I say, they have no common sense, all rascals, dull. By eating meat they are ... They may have strength of a tiger or barking capacity like a dog, but they are not human being. Useless. They cannot be used for anything human benefit-useless. We should take them like that, that 'You may be a tiger, you may be a lion, you may be a dog, but you are not a human being. We do not accept you.' A tiger is very powerful than ordinary human being, but that does not mean that a tiger is useful than the human being." He paused for a moment and then went on. "When I asked, natural answer you gave, 'Because it is disconnected with the mother.' That is natural answer. Then how you can say the life has come from matter? Immediately you are captured. Can you say like that, that life has come without life? And they are making us believe like that."

Rāmeśvara explained their idea that the body is simply matter and that life enters into it at a certain stage. "Therefore they say they can abort the baby."

"That they do not know, when the soul enters," Prabhupāda told him. "The soul enters in the first night when pregnancy begins. Otherwise how it will grow? Life begins from that point. It grows one day, two day, three day, five day, one month, three months, like that. But the growth, begins from that very point. If the life has got shelter between the two secretions of father and mother, then it grows. That is the only explanation."

"They are very bewildered," Rāmeśvara Mahārja said. "They cannot imagine how a cell within the body is growing. They cannot imagine that there is a soul within it. Or a plant from a seed. They can never understand these things. Actually it's a fact. When we studied in biology before we became devotees, they never explained how the tree comes from the seed."

Prabhupāda gave the reason. "The seed creates a favorable situation, and the life comes. On account of the life's presence, it grows, it develops. This is right explanation."

\* \* \*

Prabhupāda gave his last class to a packed house. *Guru-pūjā* vibrated through the building, the last chance for the American devotees to worship their spiritual master in person before he flew halfway across the world, leaving their country thousands of miles behind.

The verse continued with the description of Kṛṣṇa's energies, and Prabhupāda gave a beautiful example of how they are working, with the Lord Himself in the background. "He has got so unlimited potency that things are being done as if naturally, without any endeavor. Just like we see one flower growing. Very small flower, the stem is very fine and the flower is decorated different colors. But it is not ordinary thing. If you are a painter, if you paint such a flower it will take so many days. But it is coming. But don't think simply that it has come automatically. No, there is no such thing as automatically. Same, as you, when you paint a flower you have to employ so much energy, so Kṛṣṇa has also do that, the same energy. But it is because it is so natural for Kṛṣṇa, *svābhāvikī jñāna-bala-kriyā ca*. Simply by His willing it is happening. So He hasn't got to endeavor for it. That is the difference between Kṛṣṇa's activities and our activity."

He encouraged the devotees to continue the principle of associating together. "Just like you are hearing from the *śāstra* and we are speaking from the *śāstra.* This is called *sat-saṅga.* By *sat-saṅga*, by real spiritual association, by talking with them, by mixing with them, *satāṁ prasaṅgān mama vīrya-saṁvidaḥ.* Then we can learn about the unlimited potencies of Kṛṣṇa. Then it becomes very pleasing to the heart and to the ear. By *satāṁ prasaṅga.* Otherwise it is not possible. If you go to a professional reciter, it will enter in this ear and go out this ear, that's all. Because there is no life. It is business. So you cannot do business with Kṛṣṇa. Kṛṣṇa is not agreeable to this proposal. He's master. You cannot utilize Him for your service. You must engage yourself to His service, that is wanted."

\* \* \*

It seems that every time Prabhupāda holds a big initiation, he becomes afflicted with some type of physical ailment. He now has a heavy cold which is worsening. It was bad enough today to warrant him deciding not to have his usual massage with oils. Instead he had me give him a dry one so that he would not have to take a bath.

He prepared to depart from the temple by 6:00 p.m. for the evening flight to London. His GBC and senior men, however, came to petition him to remain in New York and rest until he got his health back. Some suggested that he retire from all travel and engagements for a few months. They said that even the airlines advise against traveling with a cold. Air conditioning and pressurized cabins have adverse effects, especially on the ears, which become blocked during descent. Having a cold makes it difficult to clear them, and the pressurization brings dizziness and sometimes air-sickness.

But His Divine Grace politely shrugged aside all their suggestions as he waited by the elevator door. He stepped inside, surrounded by as many *sannyāsīs* and GBC men that could fit in with him, and began the descent. He turned to them and said with complete clarity and gravity, "I simply want the benediction, like Arjuna, to fight for Kṛṣṇa to the last breath." He said it with such deep conviction that we all fell utterly silent in appreciation of his full surrender to the Lord and the great sacrifice he continues to make in the service of Kṛṣṇa, for our and the world's benefit.

As he exited through the front entrance, Prabhupāda turned to Tamal Krishna Goswami, Ādi-keśava Swami and the other temple managers and told them, "Now we have this building the Deities must never be moved again."

Our party is reduced once more to Pradyumna, his wife and child, and myself. Pālikā's tenure is over, and when we arrive in England Harikeśa Swami will resume his former cooking duties. Viśākhā and Rakṣaṇa's assignments were for North America only. Gurudāsa Swami has received an invitation to preach in England, and so he is coming with us. Srutadeva dāsa and his family from Baltimore are taking up a new service in England and are also joining our flight.

Scores of devotees accompanied Prabhupāda to the airport, holding *kīrtana* and remaining with him until the last moment at the boarding gate. At 8:00 p.m. we departed New York for London.

\* \* \*

Once we had settled in on the flight, I read out a letter which Puṣṭa Kṛṣṇa Mahārāja had given me just before we left. He had written it on Ratha-yātrā day but he had requested me to wait until after Prabhupāda's departure before reading it to him. Prabhupāda listened carefully as Puṣṭa described how he found himself now struggling to maintain his spiritual consciousness. "As of late I have been battling with the material energy and I fear that my consciousness has been dangerously polluted in the struggle. My memory of substantive reality has given way to hopelessness and fatigue under the heavy pressing of the whirlwind modes of material nature. I feel as though I have slipped from the safety of the transcendental boat and I am being swallowed up by the waves of futility and despair. Desires have entered my mind from all directions and it has been a weary struggle against fate."

He said he realized that he must have brought this upon himself but declared, "I do not have the strength to wage war any longer. ... But somehow by a shred of Your Loving Mercy I am hanging on to Your Lotus Feet and praying for these terrible phenomenon to pass." He finished by making a plea for Prabhupāda's blessings to carry on, and to give him the strength "to endure this brutal onslaught."

It was yet another headache, yet another disappointment, yet another senior *sannyāsī* disciple experiencing spiritual difficulty. Prabhupāda simply shook his head and murmured, "He is not sincere." Then he turned away, chanting softly on his beads.

## 4: London

## July 21st, 1976

The overnight flight to London was extremely difficult for Śrīla Prabhupāda. It seems that at night airlines lower the cabin temperature. Racked by a heavy cold, Prabhupāda spent practically the whole flight lying down, coughing up large amounts of mucus every few minutes. In fact, he hardly moved at all during the six and a half hour flight.

In the morning, as arrival into London neared, the airline served breakfast. Prabhupāda tried to eat a little fruit, but he found it very difficult. He was feeling so ill that he called for Gurudāsa Mahārāja, asking him to arrange a wheelchair for his arrival.

The plane touched down at 7:30 a.m. and Gurudāsa Mahārāja immediately disembarked to get a wheelchair, leaving Śrīla Prabhupāda to wait on the plane. After only a few minutes delay Prabhupāda changed his mind about waiting and began to walk Heathrow Airport's long corridors toward immigration. He was so ill that he swayed slightly from side to side and had to pause several times to steady himself. I kept right at this side, afraid he might collapse, but Prabhupāda didn't want to stop and there was nowhere to sit down.

Gurudāsa returned after five minutes informing us that the airport would supply a wheelchair, but only to the plane itself. They would not send it down the corridor. Not wanting to go all the way back, Prabhupāda continued walking. Two policemen joined us, presumably having been informed that there was a potential emergency. They didn't speak to us, but kept close behind, walking at a respectful but watchful distance, accompanying Prabhupāda all the way to the immigration desk.

At the counter there were seats, so Prabhupāda sat down and I went forward with his passport. I requested the young immigration official to please hurry because Prabhupāda was sick. Śrīla Prabhupāda's passport is thick and has three sections to it, so I patiently stood as the man looked through the whole passport trying to find the visa. Rather than ask if I knew where it was, he turned to the very back and began to look through again. It was apparent that he was taking his time simply to confirm who was in charge. Becoming exasperated, I reached out, took the passport from him and opened it immediately to the visa. Then gave it back. This annoyed the man. In a fit of petulance he grabbed his rubber stamp and poked it in my face. "'Ere, why don't you stamp it as well, eh?" he shouted childishly. "Go on! Sign it, why don't you sign it as well?"

When the policemen looked at him disapprovingly, he cooled right down and stamped the visa. Then, amazingly, as he handed back the passport, he said, "'Ere, isn't that the author of the *Bhagavad-gītā As It Is*?"

That such an apparent rascal would know the *Gītā*, let alone its author, was astonishing to me. I said, "Yes, it is. How do you know him?" The man said he had purchased a copy of the *Gītā* on Oxford Street and recognized Śrīla Prabhupāda from his picture.

I thought, "Well maybe there's hope yet that he can redeem himself." I told him that Prabhupāda would be speaking on the *Gītā* during his stay, and invited the man to Bhaktivedanta Manor to hear him.

He gave me a smile and thanked me, and with that we were through.

Leaving the policemen behind, Prabhupāda proceeded through the gate. The local GBC, Jayatīrtha prabhu, Mukunda dāsa and Harikeśa Swami headed the large crowd of joyous devotees greeting His Divine Grace. Blissfully unaware of Śrīla Prabhupāda's condition, they stepped forward and draped him with colorful garlands of roses and carnations. Rohiṇīnandana dāsa walked alongside holding an elaborately sequined yellow satin umbrella over Prabhupāda's head and despite his weak condition, Prabhupāda received their offerings gracefully with a smile and *praṇāmas.*

I quickly informed Jayatīrtha that Śrīla Prabhupāda was very sick and requested him to take us to the Manor without delay. He escorted Prabhupāda directly to a waiting Rolls Royce, which was owned and driven by an Indian life member, Mr. Patel.

With Prabhupāda and Jayatīrtha in the back and Harikeśa and me in the front, we set off on the hour long drive to the Manor. After a mere ten minutes Prabhupāda suddenly asked to stop the car. Pulling up at the roadside, he opened the door and vomited. It was alarming because it consisted more of thick, yellow bile and mucus rather than food waste. All we could do was continue on as quickly as possible to get Śrīla Prabhupāda to the Manor where he could rest.

A few minutes later I looked around to check on His Divine Grace and was shocked to see Prabhupāda gagging and going through the motions of throwing up without actually doing so. He was gesturing with his hand, moving it in a circular motion from his stomach up to his mouth and back. I shouted to Mr. Patel to stop immediately, and Prabhupāda just got the door open in time before vomiting once more. It was all the more distressing because there was nothing any of us could do to relieve him. Thankfully, we reached the Manor without further incident.

Bhaktivedanta Manor  
Letchmore Heath, Hertfordshire

Since Prabhupāda's quarters are on the upper floor, he was faced with a steep climb up a wide wooden staircase. He stood for a minute at the bottom while we quickly procured a chair, with the idea of carrying him up on it. He actually sat down on it, but as I fumbled around trying to coordinate how to lift it with two men holding the front legs and me holding the back, Prabhupāda lost patience. Without a word, he stood up, climbed the stairs and left us behind holding the empty seat.

Entering his rooms, he immediately took rest for the remainder of the day. He took no *prasādam*, no massage and received no visitors. He did, however, see Nirañjana dāsa, an young Indian college student, and one of his oldest disciples here, Kṣīrodakaśāyī Viṣṇu dāsa, a middle-aged Indian businessman who joined in London when the devotees were first starting up. He and his wife Kīrtimā dāsī were initiated in 1969. He was sitting out on the lawns and Prabhupāda saw him through the window and had him brought up. While Prabhupāda rested in bed he discussed with them whether a Gujarati Āyurvedic doctor could be brought. Then Kṣīrodakaśāyī Viṣṇu had his son bring from their home in London the Āyurvedic medicine, *Cyavana-prasha,* which is good for congestions and chest ailments and acts as a general tonic, as well as some Āyurvedic cough drops. Nirañjana also gave Prabhupāda a powdered medicine called *Sitopalādi-cūrṇa* which he mixed with honey and crushed cardamon into a paste. In addition we made a hot ginger brew with a little honey for him. Prabhupāda requested that we give him these medicines every day, as they seemed to have a salutary effect.

The British weather certainly doesn't seem conducive to Prabhupāda's quick recovery. Although it is mid-July and there has been a drought here for the past two months, the daytime is barely warm and it grew surprisingly chilly in the evening.

## July 22nd, 1976

After his prolonged rest, Prabhupāda seems to have recovered a little this morning. Although he decided to greet the Deities, it was a great strain on him. He had heart palpitations coming back up the staircase. He is still very weak. Later he attempted to eat some breakfast, but managed only two spoonfuls of fruit.

He refused his massage, and bathed by wiping himself with a sponge. He ate no lunch, save for a couple of small spoonfuls of *khicharī* brought by Kṣīrodakaśāyī Viṣṇu prabhu, which Prabhupāda ate while sitting up on the side of his bed, the plate on his lap.

During the day he called in Harikeśa Mahārāja, and told him that he wanted to return immediately to Bombay, for the climate there suited him much more favorably. Extensive inquiries, however, indicated that there were no airplane seats available until the 26th, so Prabhupāda put off making a decision for the time being.

\* \* \*

After resting all afternoon Śrīla Prabhupāda called in Harikeśa Mahārāja and Jayatīrtha prabhu, who has just taken over as the GBC here since April. He preached and chatted for a couple of hours, which was very encouraging to everyone. Though very ill, he could not resist talking about Lord Kṛṣṇa and preaching to us.
