"Yes," Prabhupāda said. "These rooms were broken. So they told me that 'You can repair these, and whatever you like, you can give.' So I thought, 'Don't need much space.' Before me there was a tenant in that other room, he was paying three rupees. So I thought, 'Two rooms, but I have spent money. So I'll give him five.' Now I am giving them ten rupees."

"To retain it."

"Yes."

"Sometimes the devotees go down there and clean out the rooms," I told him, "and they have *kīrtana* there sometimes. I think this is the first book that someone included this photo."

"Yes. It was very calm and quiet. And people used to offer obeisances from outside because they knew. Practically everyone knew me. So they used to offer ..."

"You were very well known in Vṛndāvana before you came?"

"Not very well known, but people knew me."

"Because you were writing?"

"Yes."

"Or because of your ambition to come to the West?"

"No, at that time there was no such thing," Prabhupāda replied. "I was living there, retired man."

"So when you went to Vṛndāvana, you'd given up the idea of coming to the West?"

"No, coming to the West, the idea was there, but I was planning how to go, how to go there, how to preach there, how to take some books, how to bring them—everything alone ..."

"So as soon as you had some books then you were ..."

"Yes. Then I decided. Everything was being dictated by superior."

With Śrīla Prabhupāda in such a congenial mood, I took the courage to broach something Harikeśa once mentioned to me. "I was told that one day you were told by Rūpa Gosvāmī that you must go."

Prabhupāda's mood changed slightly. "But that was open secret," he said dismissively. "Everyone knew." Then he changed the subject.

## July 27th, 1976

Once more, Prabhupāda spent a quiet day, avoiding too much physical activity. He remained in his room during the Deity greeting, *guru-pūjā* and class. But he allowed Jayatīrtha and Bhagavān prabhus to come in his room for a relaxed discussion while the devotees carried on the program without him.

George Harrison's visit prompted some talk about artists. Prabhupāda explained that in India the artistic class are considered *śūdras*, not a very high-class profession. He said a hundred years ago Girish Chandra Ghosh tried to introduce theatrical performances with both men and women actors, in imitation of the Europeans. "So he wanted to invite woman artist. Not a single woman joined. Who will go to public stage to dance, respectable girl? They'll never. That is hundred years."

He recalled that even forty years ago he knew a respectable family who rejected the notion of teaching their daughter to dance and sing. "The girl was to be married, and it is the custom in India, the bridegroom's party comes to see the girl, whether she is right. Similarly, the girl's party goes to see the boy. So they came to see my friend's daughter, and the daughter is very beautiful, rich man's daughter. So one of the bridegroom's party questioned, 'You know how to dance?' That was the question to the girl: 'You have learned something about dancing and singing?'

"So she was my friend Mukunda Mati's daughter. His elder brother was there. He became very angry, that 'This rascal is asking our daughter whether she knows dancing and singing.' He took it as insult, that 'Respectable family, daughter should learn how to dance, how to sing?' So immediately he protested, 'No, no, no. She does not know how to dance, how to sing. She's not meant for that purpose. We like, of course, a young girl dancing and singing, but we cannot teach our family members. We spend for that outside. You cannot expect our Mullik's family daughter dancing and singing.' Actually dancing, singing? What is this nonsense? For a respectable family? It is meant for the low-class professional. Pay them, they will dance. Or go to some prostitute, she will dance.

"Among the theatrical, Girish Chandra Ghosh could not get a single response from any respectable family. Then he had to seek some young girl from the prostitute class. They became later on famous artists, Kusumkarī Dāsī. Nowadays it has become a fashion that aristocratic family should join this cinema and spoil their character."

Bhagavān said that the artistic class is very influential these days.

Using George as an example, Prabhupāda acknowledged the fact, explaining, "Somehow or other get money, you become a big man. There is no question of culture or anything. That is stated in the *Bhāgavata.* Money will be the criterion—no family, culture, education. These things will not be taken into account. If you have got money, then you are big man. Nevermind what you are. Therefore people are after money. Who is going to be *brāhmaṇa*? If you become a perfect *brāhmaṇa,* who will care for you? Nobody is interested to become a *brāhmaṇa*. 'Why we shall become *brāhmaṇa*? For starvation?' Nowadays the colleges they're not interested in art, philosophy, English literature. They go for technical, how they will get more money."

Remembering Professor O'Connell in Toronto, he said, "Some of the doctor, professor, they came to request us to give our student; they are not getting student. And after few years they'll be all dismissed, who will pay them? Hayagrīva told me. He's not getting any job. There is another, Dr. Henderson, he's also not getting any job. He's selling insurance. And Bon Mahārāja, his institute is suffering from the very beginning till now, simply begging, begging and paying, paying the professor. No student. First of all he started Vaiṣṇava philosophy, so doctorate, Ph.D. So especially in India, who is going to take Ph.D. in Vaiṣṇava philosophy and starve? So this is failure. It is already failure, but he is persistent."

Bhagavān said people are very surprised that we are not starving.

"Why we shall starve?" Prabhupāda asked. "We are, rather, inviting, 'Come here, live comfortably. You chant Hare Kṛṣṇa.' When I see so many young boys are taking *prasādam,* I become so happy that they are having *prasādam* and good chance for chanting Hare Kṛṣṇa, that's all."

Speaking of *prasādam*, Prabhupāda turned to me and said that some watermelon juice he had taken yesterday evening had "created havoc" during the night. He asked for vegetable soup for his breakfast.

He went on, observing that as long as people are not enlightened about the science of spirit, they will remain in a defeated position. "So we have to now increase our scope. Everything we have got."

It didn't matter which political system people followed, either communist or capitalist, they were all defeated. "Our program is solid, but if we have to argue with animals, that is a different thing. Otherwise any human being, they will accept. But the modern civilization means to keep the people in general in animal platform, that's all, and cheat them. Now there is drought; there is no rain. What the capitalists or communists can do in this connection? If they are able to present any program how to counteract? Then where is your progress?"

I pointed out that the communists were buying wheat from the West because there was no rainfall.

Jayatīrtha added that another of their problems was the ordinary men and the farmers' disinclination to work. "They have to give all the fruit away. So because they are *karmīs,* they want the fruit. The state is taking the fruit; therefore they don't want to work. They have no incentive."

"'I'll work and you'll enjoy.' Why shall they work?" Prabhupāda said. "That is natural tendency. This can be possible only for Kṛṣṇa. 'I'll work; Kṛṣṇa will enjoy.' That's all. That is only possible in Kṛṣṇa consciousness."

He gave Arjuna as the prime example of someone willingly sacrificing everything for the satisfaction of Kṛṣṇa. "We cannot find this philosophy in the material world that 'I shall work, and so many will be satisfied.' That is not possible. 'If I work, I must be satisfied.' So these communists, everyone will show that 'I have no capacity.' So the production will reduce; and they'll have to beg."

Jayatīrtha said they were now introducing capitalistic-style incentives in many of the communist countries, in order to induce the people to work.

Prabhupāda said that would not work, that the introduction of Kṛṣṇa consciousness would. "They'll have to learn how to love Kṛṣṇa, and for Kṛṣṇa they are prepared to do anything. That is philosophy." He asked Harikeśa Mahārāja to look up a verse in the *Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam* which Harikeśa read out loud. "The supreme occupation, *dharma,* for all humanity is that by which men can attain to loving devotional service unto the transcendent Lord. Such devotional service must be unmotivated and uninterrupted in order to completely satisfy the self."

Prabhupāda said, "So the communist teaching that 'You love Lenin,' and the capitalist teaching that, 'You love Washington. So nobody's satisfied. Unless the love comes to Kṛṣṇa, there is no question of satisfied. There must be defect, because the love is reposed in some defective or imperfect personality. It may be Lenin or it may be Washington—it doesn't matter, he's imperfect.

"Love is there. Otherwise why so many people are working? But because it is misplaced, they are not satisfied. Therefore it is stated, *adhokṣaje,* this word, is used. They may say that 'Where is God?' And therefore the word is *adhokṣaje:* beyond your sense perception. Everything is within sense perception. So therefore this very word is used, that 'You cannot see, you cannot perceive, but still, you have to love Him.' They say, therefore, that this Kṛṣṇa consciousness, it is some ideal, imagination."

He explained that even if people criticize us that Kṛṣṇa cannot be seen, we can reverse that argument. "'You do not see Lenin. Why you are worshiping? Is Lenin present before you? So why you are worshiping?' You'll see. You have got, in Moscow got, every street corner a big picture. If somebody argues, 'Where is Lenin? Why you are worshiping? You cannot see Lenin ... ' Because they say, 'Where is your Kṛṣṇa? You are worshiping a statue,' so we can say the same thing, 'Where is your Lenin? The statue, it is?' In the airport station, street crossing and everywhere there is picture. And they go to worship Lenin's tomb every day. Many other fools also go there, tourists, that Red Square. They tried in India for Jawaharlal Nehru's tomb, for Gandhi's tomb. So in the beginning there was little crowd, now nobody goes. But in Vṛndāvana, Govindajī's temple, Krishna-Balarām temple, without invitation-crowd. This is culture."

Bhagavān added, "Marx, he has written only little book, and you have written so many books."

"What does he know," Prabhupāda scoffed, "that he'll write? He can bluff people, that's all. Here is Vyāsadeva, *vidvān*." Again he quoted the *Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam:* "*Anarthopaśamaṁ sākṣād bhakti-yogam adhokṣaje*/ *lokasyājānato vidvāṁś cakre sātvata-saṁhitām.*"

Harikeśa read the translation: "The material miseries of the living entity, which are superfluous to him, can be directly mitigated by the linking process of devotional service. But the mass of people do not know this, and therefore the learned Vyāsadeva compiled this Vedic literature, which is in relation to the Supreme Truth."

"So here is *vidvān,*" Prabhupāda said, "and there is a rascal. He does not know how people will be helped."

He added that the *karmīs* merely theorize; however people should see that we are doing something very practical. "So expand this farming project, self-help and peaceful life for spiritual culture." He lauded the Pennsylvania farm as the best organized of all our farming projects. In contrast to his vision of a peaceful agrarian life he warned that unemployment in the industrial society would become a great catastrophe and cause civil unrest. "They will create havoc. This is artificial. They are increasing the production of tire tube and lid. So who will purchase? Nobody lives in the tire tube. Therefore unemployment. So therefore reduce production. You cannot go on increasing. It is very artificial civilization."

Our farms he said, would be a natural alternative. "Here so far milk and food grains are concerned, whatever sumptuously you want to eat, eat. Balance you can keep stock. The milk can be converted into ghee, then keep stock, and the grains can be stocked. Whenever you like, you just grind the grains and have to eat, *halavā.* If you have got excess, you can distribute free *prasādam.* 'Come on.' You make friends."

\* \* \*

A Māyāvādī, Swami Satyāmṛtānanda, visited Prabhupāda at about 11:00 a.m. Prabhupāda received him in the airy precincts of his *darśana* room. They conversed in Hindi together, exchanging some preliminary niceties as the Swami got seated. He was friendly and complimentary about Śrīla Prabhupāda's work and ISKCON. He said that he had visited the Manor once before and wherever he traveled he visited the ISKCON centers and tried to help. Some months back he had received our devotees at his *āśrama* in Haridwar, and he said he knew Brahmānanda, having met him in Mombassa. He asked how Śrīla Prabhupāda was.

Śrīla Prabhupāda explained that his health was not good and he was suffering from "cough and fever."

Satyāmṛtānanda, while continuing to compliment Śrīla Prabhupāda's work, said that he was planning to open a small center here in London. He suggested that his society and Śrīla Prabhupāda's could work together.

Prabhupāda, while remaining cordial, showed no enthusiasm whatever for his proposal. "Our preaching is of Kṛṣṇa," he told him frankly. "*Kṛṣṇas tu bhagavān svayam.* But they are not all accepting. They are saying that we are sectarian. They are thinking that Kṛṣṇa and all the gods are the same. They believe everybody is God. But we don't believe. *Kṛṣṇas tu bhagavān svayam.* We don't agree with what you all are saying."

The Swami admitted, "Yes, there are some little differences." But his mood showed that he didn't think they were of any importance.

Prabhupāda disagreed. "So if these are the differences then how can we work together?"

"We can work together wherever we agree with each other," Satyāmṛtānanda smiled.

Prabhupāda maintained his dour countenance. "No, it is not possible. We don't believe in this hodgepodge—he is God, they are God, we are God, all gods the same."

Satyāmṛtānanda tried to adjust by verifying that in the scriptures "*deva upasana*" was recommended, but Śrīla Prabhupāda explained that this was for the less intelligent persons. "It is for *murkha*," he said, quoting from *Bhagavad-gītā*. "A person who is a *murkha*, he worships the demigods."

"But there is the *Devi Bhāgavata*," Satyāmṛtānanda pointed out, trying to remain courteous.

"Yes," Prabhupāda conceded, "it is there. It is not that no worship is allowed. But the person who is doing the worship, he is *murkha*."

Satyāmṛtānanda quoted a few Sanskrit *ślokas* to better establish his case and Prabhupāda shook his head in polite disagreement. "That is another discussion. If I say something you will get angry. So I don't want to say more."

Satyāmṛtānanda had not come to argue but to get help, so he didn't pursue his line of argument. He tried to keep it friendly by adopting the usual Māyāvādī stance that whatever one was doing, that was fine. Thus he began to reassure Śrīla Prabhupāda, "No, that's all right, you are doing the very best thing."

"I simply accept whatever is in scripture," Prabhupāda said. "*Kṛṣṇas tu bhagavān svayam.* We cannot compromise."

As Satyāmṛtānanda continued to waggle his head and smile Prabhupāda gave him assurance that we do not disregard the demigods, we offer them all respects. "*Tṛṇād api sunīcena taror api sahiṣṇunā*. ... Śrī Caitanya Mahāprabhu says even the ant on the ground should be given respect so what to speak of big, big demigods. We respects all others. But Kṛṣṇa is the all in all." Quoting the *Brahma-saṁhitā* verse which describes Durgādevī as the shadow of the internal energy of Kṛṣṇa, Prabhupāda said, "*Icchānurūpam* means He is independent. *Mayādhyakṣeṇa prakṛtiḥ* \[Bg. [9.10](https://vedarama.com/en/books/bg/9.10)\] *māyā* is working under His superintendence. So they all say that Durgā is the same as Kṛṣṇa and others, but we don't believe in that. They are not all the same."

Satyāmṛtānanda continued to shrug and smile, as if to say that he didn't hold it against Śrīla Prabhupāda for his dedication to a particular line of thought. "Its OK. Everyone has their own beliefs, so that's OK."

Prabhupāda continued to quote evidence of Kṛṣṇa's supremacy from *Bhagavad-gītā* indirectly telling his visitor that even the basic literature makes it obvious. "We don't know all big, big scriptures. Whatever Bhagavān says in *Bhagavad-gītā* is enough for us, and by that the work is going on."

"It is a good work," the Swami agreed.

And although Satyāmṛtānanda wasn't really interested in hearing, Prabhupāda continued to make his point. "Bhagavān Himself says *mattaḥ parataraṁ nānyat*, so why they have thought about something else? We will give respect to everyone, but the *pūrṇa bhagavān* is Kṛṣṇa. *Sarva pūrṇa puruṣottama. Ete cāṁśa-kalāḥ puṁsaḥ kṛṣṇas tu bhagavān svayam*. All others are Bhagavān's *avatāra;* some are *aṁśa* and some are *kalā*, but Kṛṣṇa is the original."

Satyāmṛtānanda asked if we consider Rāma to be just Balarāma.

Prabhupāda told him that no, we say that Rāma is also Rāma as well as Balarāma since Rāma is also Bhagavān. "Our temple in Bombay will have Sīta-Rāma also; *rāmādi-mūrtiṣu kalā-niyamena tiṣṭhan nānāvatāram akarod bhuvaneṣu kintu/ kṛṣṇa svayaṁ samabhavat paramaḥ pumān yo govindam ādi-puruṣaṁ tam aham bhajāmi-kṛṣṇas tu bhagavān svayam*. So *pūrṇa bhagavān* means Kṛṣṇa. Arjuna also says *paraṁ brahma paraṁ dhāma*. So this is the instruction and this is what we are spreading. It is not difficult. The big, big *ācāryas* can offer obeisances and *praṇāma* and the common person also can do the same."

Point made, Śrīla Prabhupāda switched to a lighter subject, asking the Swami how long he was going to stay in London and informing him of his own travels and the recent New York Ratha-yātrā. Satyāmṛtānanda urged Prabhupāda to try to bring the Muslims in and Prabhupāda gladly informed him that he already had a temple in Iran run by his Iranian disciple Atreya Ṛṣi. "His name previously was Attar," he laughed. "So we have called him Atreya Ṛṣi."

"Do they wear the *dhotī, tilaka* and all these things?" the Swami asked.

"Oh, yes," Śrīla Prabhupāda told him. "I don't make them my disciple unless they follow our regulations. Whoever wants to be my disciple, they have to follow these things—no illicit sex, no gambling, no meat-eating, no drinking, not even tea or coffee. That is little difficult for people to come because they have to follow these principles."

"Well you have done a very good job. You already have more than ten thousand followers so that is not a small amount." The Swami invited Śrīla Prabhupāda to come with his disciples to visit his place in Haridwar when he comes to India.

"Yes, we will come," Prabhupāda said. "Now I am over eighty years, so I am getting weaker but still I am traveling to all our centers, two, three days, so time is passing." Indicating we few disciples by his side he went on, "He is from America, he is from Europe—they all are helping to print and sell books. We are selling daily $60,000 worth of books, every day, minimum, in Spanish, German, Japanese—in all languages we are spreading these books."

So after a gracious half hour meeting, Swami Satyāmṛtānanda took his leave promising to see Prabhupāda in Bombay to take him to Haridwar. "Hare Kṛṣṇa, Hare Kṛṣṇa," he said as he got up to leave.

"*Jaya*," Prabhupāda replied. "Hare Kṛṣṇa."

\* \* \*

In mid-afternoon Mukunda prabhu introduced Śrīla Prabhupāda to Mike Robinson, a young interviewer from the London Broadcasting Company. It is a local radio station that hosts a two and a half hour religious program every Sunday. Prompted by the daily sight of our devotees dancing and chanting down Oxford Street, Mike felt his listeners would be interested to hear about us.

By deflecting a question about the history of the movement to Mukunda, Prabhupāda made it clear he wanted to speak on the philosophy at the outset. Mike was quick to adjust, and decided he would interview Mukunda separately afterwards. He then asked Śrīla Prabhupāda, "Can you tell me what you believe, what is the philosophy of the Hare Kṛṣṇa movement?"

Prabhupāda corrected him that there was no question of belief; Kṛṣṇa consciousness was a science. As proof, he explained the process of transmigration of the soul. He also had Harikeśa read out *Bhagavad-gītā* verse [2.20](https://vedarama.com/en/books/bg/2.20).

Mike asked, "So can you explain to me just a bit more, if the soul is undying, does everybody's soul go to be with God when they die?"

"Not necessarily," Prabhupāda replied. "If he qualifies himself in this life to go back home, back to Godhead, then he can go. If he does not qualify himself, he gets another material body—and there are 8,400,000 different forms of body. And according to his desire and *karma* \[activities\], the laws of nature give him a body." He stressed that because everyone is under the laws of material nature, no one is free. "So this next birth will be decided according to my activities this life, sinful or pious, like that."

Mike was following carefully, and was quick-witted enough to ask, "You said nobody is free. But you are saying that if we live a good life we in some way determine our future as well?"

Prabhupāda confirmed that and Mike continued, "So we are free to choose in so far as what we believe important. I mean religion is important, because if we believe in God and live a good life ..."

Prabhupāda interrupted him, repeating what he said at the outset. "Don't bring this question, belief. It is law. Just like there is government—you believe or not believe, who cares for you? That is government."

"I see," said Mike. "Does it matter what religion you believe?"

"It is not a question of which religion," Prabhupāda said. "It is a question of science what is your position." He pointed out that whether a Christian or a Hindu, every child becomes a boy. It is nature's law.

"So you are saying there is only one God."

"Yes," Prabhupāda answered.

"Can you explain to me then what difference it makes being a member of the Hare Kṛṣṇa movement?"

"Hare Kṛṣṇa movement," Prabhupāda told him, "means one who is serious to understand this science, he's member of the Hare Kṛṣṇa movement. This is the beginning of education, that you are a spirit soul. Our mission is to educate."

Prabhupāda then described how the soul is carried by the subtle mind from one body to another. Mike quickly picked up on the implications. "Are you saying that we were perhaps something else before we were born as well? And we keep coming back in something else next time?"

"Oh, yes."

"And how long does this go on?" Mike asked.

"This is going on because you are eternal," Prabhupāda explained. "According to your work, you are simply changing body. Therefore you should be educated how to stop this business, how to remain in our original, spiritual body. And that is Kṛṣṇa consciousness movement."

"Oh, I see," Mike said. "So if I gain Kṛṣṇa consciousness, I wouldn't have to have the threat of coming back as a dog or something like that."

"No, no." Prabhupāda smiled in agreement and had Harikeśa read out a second verse, *Bhagavad-gītā* [4.9](https://vedarama.com/en/books/bg/4.9).

Prabhupāda's frequent use of *śāstra* intrigued Mike. "Now we've had two readings from your scriptures. Where do these scriptures come from? Can you explain that briefly?"

Prabhupāda obliged, using a wonderful analogy. "This is coming from Vedic literature, which is eternal. When there is creation, this material creation, anything, material creation ... Just like this microphone is a material creation. So how to deal with it, there is some literature. Is it not?"

"How to deal with the microphone?" Mike asked.

"Yes. There is some literature."

"Yes, that's right, there is."

"Yes," Prabhupāda said. "So that literature comes along with the creation of the microphone. So similarly, the Vedic literatures comes immediately with the creation."

"I see. So these scriptures have been in existence since we have, is what you're saying," Mike nodded. "What about other scriptures? Other religions have got their scriptures, do you believe, do you accept them?"

Prabhupāda stayed with the same example. "The literature issued along with the manufacturer of this microphone is bona fide. So if anyone follows that bona fide literature, he can deal with it. Otherwise, a bogus."

Having been previously primed by the devotees, Mike moved to a different subject. "I see. Well, if we could take something which I believe you feel very strongly about, and that's some of the other Eastern cults and gurus."

Prabhupāda wasn't that keen to discuss others, but he still responded. "So far I know, they do not know anything. They simply come and bluff and cheat, that's all."

"I see," said Mike. "What are the big differences that you seem to be ...?"

"The difference is," Prabhupāda said, "they are not following the original literature; they are manufacturing their own literature. That is the difference. Not authorized."

"I'm noticing that you are stressing very much science and rational thinking," Mike said, "and they very often stress feeling, which doesn't seem to ..."

"Yes. When there is something wrong, you just consult the original literature, not any literature issued by a bogus man," Prabhupāda said.

"Can you explain to me, then, the place of feeling in your religion. The place of emotions?"

"Our feeling is that we are dealing with the genuine thing, that's all," Prabhupāda said with easy confidence.

Mike switched topics, focusing more on Prabhupāda himself. "Why was it that you left until you were so late in life before you founded this Movement?"

Prabhupāda didn't mind the personal nature of this enquiry, and answered him simply. "I must be prepared, I must be bona fide to preach. If one is going to pass M.A. examination he must be qualified. Not that all of a sudden one becomes M.A."

"Can you tell me how you feel led? You know, how you are guided in what you do?"

Again Prabhupāda answered in a straightforward manner. "Well, there are these books, just like I told you, the literature."

"So it's from your literature that you've learned that you've got to do this."

"Yes, we have got so many literatures. We are explaining in English. Guide is ... it is not manufactured. The guide is from the beginning. Simply one has to take that guidance, then everything's all right. And if we manufacture guidance, then it is spoiled. Just like in the literature of this microphone, you say that this should be like this, this should be like this, number two should be by the side of number four. You cannot make any change, then it is spoiled."

Mike had prepared for his interview by studying some of Prabhupāda's books. "One of the things you say is that 'Religion without a rational basis is just sentiment.' Can you explain that to us, and the converse of it?"

Prabhupāda appreciated his question. "Just like most religions, they say, 'We believe.' So what is this believe? You may believe something which is not naturally correct. Just like some of the Christian people, they say, 'We believe there is no soul of the animal.' That is not correct. You have believed because you want to eat the animal. You have discovered philosophy, but that's not the fact."

"How do you know the animal has a soul?" Mike asked.

"You can know also," Prabhupāda said. "What is the difference? How do you distinguish that the animal has no soul and the man has soul?"

"I believe this Christian religion do it because their scriptures say ..."

Prabhupāda caught him out. "Again you believe, don't believe, don't believe. When you say that the animal has no soul, but you believe or you know that man has soul. So what is the distinction between the man and the animal you find so that you say the animal has no soul? What is your scientific conclusion? How do you say that animal has no soul?"

"As far as the Christian faith is concerned, doesn't it base it ...?"

"Why are you bringing Christian?" Prabhupāda challenged him.

"Well, I thought you quoted Christianity," Mike returned. "But as far as the Christian faith is concerned, don't they quote their scriptures?"

"Then it is misleading," Prabhupāda said. "As soon as you say that, 'We Christians, we believe,' then it is misbelief. It is not scientific."

"Well how does it become scientific?" Mike wanted to know.

"Scientific because the animal eats, you eat; the animal sleeps, you sleep; the animals have sex, you have sex; the animal defends, you also defend. Then where is the difference between you and the animal? Why do you say there is no soul?"

Although Mike appreciated Prabhupāda's logic, he kept trying to refer back to the Christian scriptures. Śrīla Prabhupāda however told him not to bring in the scripture. He wanted him to use his own common sense in understanding his point. He said, "Apart from your believing as Christian, as we are talking, as a scientist, how do you deny this animal has no soul?"

Since Prabhupāda had already established his credentials on the basis of scripture, Mike now sensed something to the contrary. "But ultimately you're basing all your faith factually, aren't you? On your reasoning?"

"No, no, no. It is quite logic." Prabhupāda again repeated the similarities between humans and animals. "So why do you deny this poor animal soul?"

"Well, perhaps if I put my point perhaps a slightly different way," Mike said. "This is a hypothetical situation, but if you, by your reasoning, could imagine something that seemed contrary to the scriptures that you were reading earlier ..."

"Again scripture. Why do you bring scripture?"

Mike said, "Well, I'm referring to your scripture, not ..."

"Not my scripture. It is common sense talking." Prabhupāda told him.

A bit perplexed at Prabhupāda's departure from the scriptural basis, Mike said, "Yes, but everything that you, because in ..."

"No, forget that everything. Come to the common platform of understanding. The animal is eating, you are eating; the animal sleeping, you are sleeping; the animal is defending, you are defending; the animal is having sex, you have sex; the animal have children, you have got children; you have got a living place, they have got a living place. If your body's cut, there is blood; if the animal body's cut, there is blood. So all the similarities are there. So why you deny one similarity? Analogy. Analogy means points of similarity. So this is logic. You have read logic? There is a chapter, analogy. Analogy means points of similarity. If the points of similarity are so many things, why one similarity should be avoided? That is not logic, that is not science."

Now in the spirit of things Mike presented his own converse hypothesis, that if you started from the point of saying that animals have no soul, then you would have to say that humans also have no soul. "What proof have you got then that a human being has got a soul?" he asked.

"That is, I have already begun," Prabhupāda said. "As soon as the soul is gone, what is the value of your this beautiful body? Who cares for this body? You throw it away, kick it out. And now, if I touch your hair, there will be fight!"

Mike laughed along with the rest of us.

"Yes," Prabhupāda said with a grin. "That is the distinction. The soul is there and soul is not there. As soon as soul is not there, it has no value, useless. Therefore you have to study. At the present moment people are so dull-headed, they are not taking the important point, that this body one minute ago it was so important, and now it has no value. If you kick on his face, nobody will say. But they have no brain to understand what is that thing missing, that it has become so unimportant that within a minute ... They have no brain. The so-called scientists, philosophers—all dull-headed. It is very abominable condition of society. There is no man who is real brain."

Picking up on Prabhupāda's criticism of the leaders of modern society, Mike asked, "Are you, sir, writing off all scientists because they've failed to understand the spiritual dimension in life?" Then, since Prabhupāda had been a chemist in his previous secular life, he added, "Presumably you think that science is also important, even if scientists are being dull-headed."

"Important so far. Not all-important." Prabhupāda said.

Mike now retraced his steps a little. He was still intrigued by Prabhupāda's previous insistence on the use of logic. "When we were differing a few minutes ago, you were saying don't bring the scriptures in, use common sense. But what part do the scriptures have in your religion? How important are they?"

"Our religion is science," Prabhupāda said. "When we speak that a child grows to a boy, it is science, it is not religion. Every child grows to become a boy; where is the question of religion? Every man dies; where is the question of religion? And when a man dies, the body is useless. So where is the question of religion? It is science. Either you are Christian or Hindu or Muslim, when you die your body's useless—this is science. You cannot say that 'We are Christian. Now the body is dead. Now we don't consider it as dead. We believe it is not dead.' No, it is dead. So when we speak, we speak on this basis, that the body is important—it doesn't matter whether it is Christian body or Hindu body or Muslim body—so long the soul is there. When the soul is not there, it is useless. It is applicable to everyone."

"I think I'm beginning to get, if you could explain, a bit confused. What I'd like you to explain is ..."

"We are trying to educate people on this basis."

"But that's, if I understand you correctly, you seem to be educating people on a purely scientific basis."

"Yes." Prabhupāda affirmed.

"So where does religion come into it at all?" Mike asked, his face a polite expression of puzzlement.

"Religion means also science. But they have taken religion as faith, 'I believe.' Actually, religion means ..." Prabhupāda looked in my direction. "Just like in the dictionary, you find what is the religion."

"Obeying the Supreme Person," I recalled from memory.

"Yes," Prabhupāda said to Mike. "Religion means to learn how to obey the supreme controller. That is religion. So you may be Christian, I may be Hindu, it doesn't matter. But we must accept there is a supreme controller."

Flicking through the pages of the dictionary on Prabhupāda's desk I found the reference. "It says, 'Human recognition of superhuman controlling power ..."

"Just see!" Prabhupāda interjected.

"... and especially of a personal God entitled to obedience, and effect of such recognition on the conduct of mental attitude."

"This is religion," Prabhupāda told Mike. "This is religion. So this religion is applicable to everyone, any human being. Why do you bring Christian or Hindu or Muslim, or ... ? Everyone has to accept that. That is real religion. And this is not religion: 'We believe there is no soul of the animal.' That is most unscientific. Religion means scientific understanding of the supreme controller. Immediately you have to accept. As soon as you accept there is supreme controller, so immediately as you violate the laws of the supreme controller, you are punished. That is nature's law."

"In your opinion, is it impossible for somebody to be a scientist and not to believe in God?" Mike asked.

"Unless he's a rascal, he cannot say that," Prabhupāda declared. "Scientifically, you have to accept God; you cannot deny God." Prabhupāda gave his example of Mother Nature giving birth to the various types of living beings. Then he said, "If the material nature is the mother and all these living entities are children, then where is the father?"

Mike hesitated a moment. "I don't know." Then he answered, "The father is God."

"There," Prabhupāda said, with satisfaction. "You must know there must be father. I may not know him, but without father the children cannot be brought into existence. This is science. First of all, try to understand this. The mother is there, the children are there. So there must be father. This is scientific. So who is that rascal scientist who can say, 'No, there is no father'? Then he's not a scientist, he's a rascal. How you can deny the existence of father? You may not see Him or may see Him, it doesn't matter; there must be Father. This simple understanding."

"So you completely write off anybody who says that there should be a step of faith ... ," Mike started to say.

"No faith!" Prabhupāda declared. "It is fact!"

"So you would say that science can prove that God exists?"

"Yes, here is proof. It doesn't require much proof."

Satisfied with Prabhupāda's reasoning, Mike moved on to the classic question: "Can you tell me what you believe to be the meaning of life? Why do we exist in the first place?"

Prabhupāda's reply was disarmingly simple. "Meaning of life means to enjoy. But we are in a different platform of life; therefore we are suffering instead of enjoying. But if you come to the real platform, then you enjoy." He asserted that although everyone is after enjoyment and struggling to achieve happiness, at the present moment their life is not enjoyable. He asked Mike if he agreed.

"You are saying that at the present moment we are all suffering?" Mike asked.

"Yes."

"Yes," said Mike. "I would agree with that."

"Then the question should be, 'I want to enjoy. Why am I suffering?' Then you will have to mold your real life; then you'll enjoy. And that," Prabhupāda told him, "is spiritual knowledge."

As the hour long interview came near to its close, Mike asked his final two questions, both of them addressed to Śrīla Prabhupāda's own personal spiritual status. He requested Prabhupāda to speak about the different stages of spiritual development he had been through.

Prabhupāda spoke readily. "Yes, first stage is that you are inquisitively trying to understand. This is the first stage. This is called *śraddhā,* that you have got some faith, 'What is this movement? Let me study.' This is the beginning. Then, if you are serious, then those who are cultivating this knowledge, you mix with them, try to understand how they are feeling. Then you'll feel, why not become one of them? Then when you become one of them, then all your misgivings go away. And then you become more faithful, then you get a taste. Why these boys are not going to see the cinema? They can go—other boys are going. They never ask me; neither they would like to see even. They hate. Their taste is different. Why they do not eat meat? Go to the restaurant? Their taste has changed. In this way you make progress. Firm faith, taste is changed, then God realization, then love of Godhead, the perfection. That is wanted, love of Godhead. That is first-class religion. Not that ritualistic ceremony, 'I believe,' 'This belief.' That is not religion; that is cheating. Really when you develop your love for God, that is perfection of religion."

Apparently satisfied, Mike asked his remaining question, "Perhaps finally, then, I could ask you, do you ever have any doubts?"

Prabhupāda's eyes widened. "If I have doubts, how I am preaching? That means I am cheating. And how I am writing so many books? Do you think a man with doubt can produce, in doubtful condition, he can produce so many books? Do you think like that?"

Mike became a little sheepish, especially hearing us chuckling in the background. "Well, I don't know, I just ..."

"Well, you should know!" Prabhupāda declared, his strength of conviction making us laugh.

"So you never doubt any of this, anything at all?"

Prabhupāda smiled at him. "We are sure."

The official interview over, Mike remained for a few minutes, gladly accepting a small plate of *halavā* and milk sweets. "It's lovely," he said, and asked how it was made.

"Most of our preparations are made from milk products," Prabhupāda said. "Therefore we are so much fond of cow protection. It gives the basic principle of palatable foodstuff. But these people, they do not know. They simply cut the throat of the cow and boil it and with salt!"

Mike laughed along with us as Prabhupāda continued to describe the value of mother cow. "They do not know how to keep the cow and take milk from it and prepare hundreds and thousands of nice preparations. That is a lack of civilization. Just like all the aborigines, they find an animal, kill it and eat. They do not how to utilize the animals, most aboriginals. We keep cows, we take milk, and from milk we make yogurt, we make ghee, and from ghee we prepare so many things."

"What do you do with a cow when it dies?" Mike asked. "Do you just bury it?"

Jovially Prabhupāda answered, "Yes. The cow-eaters can come and take it free of charge."

Perhaps only half-jokingly Mike replied, "Well, let me know, you know."

Prabhupāda told him of the system still current in parts of India. "You can get the skin free of charges. There is a class, when the cow dies, they are called—they are called *chāmar.* So he comes, take away the dead animal, and they eat the flesh and take the skin, make shoes. They get all, everything free. There is no question of going to the butcher's place to purchase. So this much patience they have got, that 'We want to eat this cow. All right, let us wait till her death.'

"'No, immediately!'

"Just see, what a civilization. And cow is giving milk, she is mother. Killing the mother, do you think it is civilization? Mother who has given you milk in your childhood, and maintained your life, and because she is old, cutting throat. Is that good civilization?"

Mike obviously hadn't given it much thought, but Prabhupāda's remarks made sense. "Seems silly, doesn't it," he said.

As Jayatīrtha showed him pictures of New Vrindaban, Mike asked Śrīla Prabhupāda if he found the English weather cold.

Prabhupāda, who is still coughing and full of mucus, told him, "We are accustomed to tropical climate. Heat does not disturb us, but cold disturbs us. We can tolerate extreme heat, one hundred and twenty degrees, but we cannot tolerate fifty degree cold."

Mike laughed. "That's cold!?"

As Mike finished his *prasādam* Prabhupāda had a question for him. "Why young men are attracted to, they inquire? Why young men are attracted in this Movement?"

Mike shrugged amiably. "What is the answer?"

"They are receptive," Prabhupāda told him. "Young man is blank slate. They are not sophisticated, therefore they receive very nicely. Mind is open. And they are not so sinful, because they are young."

"Not quite so defeated by material nature," I suggested.

"Yes. There is time," Prabhupāda said.

Prabhupāda encouraged Mike's receptivity and quick-wittedness. "You come here every Sunday. Take our, this *prasādam.*"

Mike thought the proposition a good one, at least in terms of getting more news stories. "I'd very much like, if I could sometime in the future, perhaps to come and interview some of the people who are here. That would be possible if sometime I could just spend the day up here and talk to some ..."

"You can live here comfortably, yes," Prabhupāda said, giving me the distinct impression he meant Mike should come for more than just an interview. Śrīla Prabhupāda mentioned how George Harrison had spent yesterday with him. Then, before sending him down to see the *ārati* ceremony in the temple below, Prabhupāda appealed to him, "I shall request you, you are young man, just try to study our philosophy. And as you are journalist, try to do some good to the people. That is your duty."

Amiable as Mike was, he remained noncommittal. "Well, certainly we're trying to present both other people's views and ..."

"Don't take it as a sectarian religious system," Prabhupāda assured him. "It is very scientific understanding for spiritual life."

Mike expressed a genuine satisfaction in having met Śrīla Prabhupāda. "Thank you very much, pleasure to meet you." Then he went off with Mukunda to view the Deities.

It was a great interview, one of the best of the tour. Mike was intelligent and quickly picked up on Prabhupāda's points. He had had no difficulty following Prabhupāda's accent or the philosophy he spoke.

Harikeśa Mahārāja and I lingered a few minutes in Prabhupāda's room, keen for more of his association and eager to offer him praise. Listening to Śrīla Prabhupāda is always nectarean, but this exchange had been particularly sweet. I said, "You're very expert. You capture them, and then you guide what they are going to say. It's perfect."

Harikeśa was also full of admiration. "I was noticing that, that when you finish speaking with somebody, although he's bewildered, all of a sudden he understands, and he becomes amazed. I mean that happens with me also. It's just, it's the most fantastic technique. You're so patient."

I recalled how he had dealt with the reporter from the Associated Press in New York, forcing him to keep with the analogies of the car and petrol, and then the breaking of bricks in prison, until he understood. "You do it in such a way that they think that they're asking very good questions from their own intelligence. Actually, you've already captured them."

Prabhupāda laughed. "He said that breaking the bricks is the business. I said the sooner you give up this, then you are happy. The *karmīs* want this, breaking the bricks. They think this is civilization. Brick, and bring more bricks and break it—that is civilization."

Harikeśa's adoration flowed copiously. "We have to get you on every radio in the world, Prabhupāda. We just have to put you on the radio everywhere."

Perhaps recognizing the physical impossibility of that, but appreciating the sentiment, Prabhupāda told him with a smile, "You do it, I give you the ideas."

Harikeśa though didn't feel it was just a question of someone speaking the philosophy; it was Śrīla Prabhupāda's own transendental personality. "Oh, everything you say is so wonderful. We have to put you on the radio. These people have no idea."

Prabhupāda chuckled. "No, thing is that I say all these things because I always think of this. I always think."

I added, "If you don't forget Kṛṣṇa, then ..."

"Yes," Prabhupāda confirmed. "You always think how to talk with these demonic people. Then Kṛṣṇa will give you intelligence."

"This is the most difficult welfare work," I suggested.

"Not difficult," Prabhupāda said. "It is easiest. But this rascal will not take the easiest."

"That's the difficulty," I said.

"Yes. They have made it difficult. Accept the supreme controller, everything is clear. Accept the father, everything is clear. There is mother, there is children—no father! How rascal they have made. How it can be? No experience, and still they will persist, 'No father. Can you show me the father?' What is this nonsense? If you do not see the father, it does not mean that there is no father? Father must be there. You may not have seen, that is different thing. And you can see the father because the father is maintaining the family order. Therefore there is father. From this simple analogy. Just like father gives money in the hand of the mother and she maintains the children's comforts. Similarly, whatever comforts we are getting, from the nature's gift, you say that is arrangement of the father. *Mayādhyakṣeṇa prakṛtiḥ sūyate sa-carācaram.* Clearly said. Father gives order, 'Nature, do this way, do this way. He's disobeying, then punish him like this, that's all. Don't give him anything. Punish him.'"

Referring to the current drought in Europe he said, "Just like nature is not supplying water. The order of Kṛṣṇa: 'Let them suffer for some time.' This is going on. You cannot check it, Father's order. Common sense. How they can deny the Supreme Father? Dull-headed fools. *Mūḍha*."

Later on Prabhupāda remarked that the LBC interview contained ninety per cent of our philosophy and should be printed in BTG.

## July 28th, 1976

After a brief *darśana* of the Deities Śrīla Prabhupāda set off in the Rolls Royce to catch the flight to Paris. A host of devotees accompanied him, this time in a more joyous mood than at our arrival, because he is at least well enough to walk and resume his travels. Our plane left in mid-morning.

## 5: Paris and New Māyāpur

## July 28th, 1976

Prabhupāda and I sat up in the first class cabin waiting for takeoff as the other passengers slowly filed past us in the aisle. One man in particular gave us an intense look. With a half-smile he suddenly bent forward and stuck his face next to mine. "How are ya, Ha-ari?" he sneered nastily, with a pronounced American accent. Then he was gone, off to his seat in the economy section. It was an unpleasant experience to say the least. Prabhupāda saw it but said nothing.

After a short flight the plane touched down at Charles de Gaulle airport. Within a few minutes we were on a moving walkway through a long airport tunnel, enroute to immigration. We were each standing about two yards apart; I was in the lead, Prabhupāda was in the middle, and Harikeśa Swami was in the rear. About halfway along the walkway's length I heard a sudden commotion behind; then Harikeśa Mahārāja and the nasty American from the plane came careening past me. Locked in an unwelcome embrace and tangled up in luggage, noisy threats and curses issued from the demon while Harikeśa reproached him.

Their little dance ended as quickly as it began; they suddenly disentangled, and the demon sped off at a fast walk, shouting obscenities and abuses at us. I was amazed, Harikeśa was irate, but Prabhupāda was serene. Harikeśa said that while standing behind Prabhupāda, he suddenly felt that he must move forward and shield him. At that very moment the American appeared from behind, deliberately trying to barge into Śrīla Prabhupāda as he went past—but he contacted Harikeśa instead.

Prabhupāda never said a word about the incident, and it was quickly forgotten. However, it stands as a pointed reminder that no matter how good one's intentions and deeds are, there is always some envious soul going out of his way to make trouble.

Many devotees, led by Bhagavān prabhu, were at the terminal, and as soon as they saw the transcendental form of Śrīla Prabhupāda they burst into *kīrtana*, offering him garlands of fragrant flowers while Bhagavān led the way out to the waiting car. From the airport Prabhupāda was driven to the Paris temple for an overnight stay.

Śrī Śrī Rādhā-Paris-īśvara Temple  
4 Rue la Sueur

As soon as he arrived Prabhupāda went into the temple room for *darśana*. The place was small, but the Deities of Śrī Śrī Rādhā-Paris-īśvara shone radiantly from Their altar.

After receiving *guru-pūjā* from the fifty or sixty devotees, Śrīla Prabhupāda gave a short speech. Allowing one of the devotees to translate sentence by sentence, he explained that Lord Viṣṇu and His potency is one. But, he explained, there is a third energy—this material world—which is a reflection of the transcendental energy. We all have to work to achieve anything in this reflection, whereas in the spiritual world everything is supplied automatically. "So the more you spiritualize the whole atmosphere," he told the devotees, "the more you become sufficient and happy. This Kṛṣṇa consciousness movement is for that purpose. People cannot understand it. They think that, 'These people are not working—simply chanting, dancing and eating.' But that is our business." He grinned and the devotees laughed. "Without working, we can have everything sufficiently.

"So stick to this Kṛṣṇa consciousness. You are already advanced. That is my request; don't deviate. You'll have never any want, that's a fact. It is not my invention, it is the statement of Kṛṣṇa. *Teṣāṁ nityābhiyuktānāṁ yoga-kṣemaṁ vahāmy aham. Nityābhiyukta,* those who are constantly engaged in Kṛṣṇa business, whatever they want, Kṛṣṇa is personally interested to supply it. So without any hesitation, stick to this Kṛṣṇa consciousness, everything will be amply supplied. Not that we shall be indolent and lazy. No. We shall utilize our energy for giving service to Kṛṣṇa. That actually we are engaged. We are not lazy. Every one of us is engaged in some sort of service for Kṛṣṇa. So that is my request, that I am now getting old, and that you stick to this principle, and you'll remain always happy."

Then he looked out over the devotees with a smile and asked, "I think this is for the fourth time I have come here? So I find you very happy. Continue, and whenever I shall come, I shall see you happy. Thank you very much."

With the devotees cheering all around him, Śrīla Prabhupāda dismounted the *vyāsāsana* and took a small elevator to the second floor. The devotees have arranged a small but comfortably appointed room for him, with an adjoining servant's room.

Due to the change in the time zone it was already 12:20 p.m. by the time we settled in. I quickly set up the dictaphone and other desk paraphernalia, and then got ready to give Śrīla Prabhupāda his massage. Harikeśa and Bhagavān made arrangements for someone to cook Prabhupāda's lunch. Bhagavān prabhu mentioned several ladies who could be possible cooks. Deciding on Parijāta dāsī, who has cooked for him before, Prabhupāda said, "All right, she cooks nice." He told them to make his regular standard fare, "not cumberous" as he put it—rice, (which he stipulated must be well cooked), vegetables, bitter melon and two or three *capātīs*. He also asked for *dāl* which he said could be of any variety, as long as it boiled nicely. "Without being boiled," he said, "it is useless."

\* \* \*

When I entered Prabhupāda's room to give his evening massage, he came out from the bathroom and went over to an open window to look out for a minute on the neighborhood. He tipped his head up slightly pointing out a few women loitering in the park opposite us. Men were walking slowly past. With a chuckle he said, "In this quarter, there are many prostitutes." Still, he didn't seem disturbed by it because, as he said, it is an important location, in the center of the city.

Prabhupāda managed to translate a little during the night, the first work he has done on his books since we left New York.

## July 29th, 1976

Early in the morning we embarked on the three hour trip to the farm. We went by car and stopped only once for a drink of water and to stretch.

La Nouvelle Māyāpur,  
Lucay-Le-Male, Valencay, Indre

The former Chateau d'Oublaise is a beautiful castle situated in the heart of the French countryside. Constructed of whitish stone with turreted roof and spires, three floors and a basement, it seems ideal for ISKCON's purposes, although it requires a good deal of renovation. We have about two hundred acres of good farmland and numerous other stone dwellings and farm buildings a little apart from the Chateau. Prabhupāda is pleased to see the devotees adopting rural life. He sees great potential for our expansion in Europe through the acquisition of such properties.

He went first to the high-ceilinged temple room and offered his prostrated obeisances to Śrī Śrī Gaura-Nitāi. Sitting on his newly constructed *vyāsāsana* carved from black and white marble he surveyed his eager followers. With a bright smile he said, "So, I am very glad to see you again in this village."

All the devotees cheered, "*Hari bol!*"

"Hare Kṛṣṇa. It was the prediction of Śrī Caitanya Mahāprabhu that in every village, in every town on the surface of the globe, there will be preaching of Sri Caitanya Mahāprabhu's name and the Hare Kṛṣṇa *mahā-mantra.* So by your transcendental endeavor it is being fulfilled, otherwise who expected that in this remote village of France, Hare Kṛṣṇa *mahā-mantra* would be chanted? When Caitanya Mahāprabhu said in every village, in every town, He did not mean that every village and every town in India. He specifically says *pṛthivīte,* means on the surface of the globe."

Speaking in short phrases so that his words could be translated, Śrīla Prabhupāda told us, "So the purpose is that without spreading of this Kṛṣṇa consciousness movement nobody can become happy. That's a fact. The opportunity of human form of life is systematically being refused by the modern civilization. This material activity only for the bodily comforts of life, that is not human civilization. Human civilization means the human being must know the supreme controller and the aim of life. The real fact is that God is there, the supreme controller, and we, living entities, we are His parts and parcels. As parts and parcels of God, we, being separated, we are suffering. An example can be given in this connection, just like a small child is the part and parcel of the body of the mother. So the child is happy when the child is on the lap of the mother. That means the part and the whole must live together. Then there is happiness. Otherwise, there is distress. The modern godless civilization is making the part and the whole separated. Therefore the whole condition is chaotic. You have got experience in your this part of the globe. Within fifty years there have been two big, big wars and ... many other parts also. People are not in happiness on account of godlessness. So actually if we want to be happy in this life and the next life, then we must take to Kṛṣṇa consciousness. And it is not at all difficult—simply chant the Hare Kṛṣṇa *mantra*. So I am very glad that you are accustomed to chant this Hare Kṛṣṇa *mahā-mantra.* Stick to it and you'll all be happy."

His brief words were enough to satisfy the devotees. Anticipating the possibility of him not coming due to his illness, they were jubilant to have him now sitting before them. To their cheers, and a loud *kīrtana* led by Pṛthu-putra Swami, Prabhupāda went up the old elevator (which Bhagavān said they had only just got working in the last couple of days) to the second floor where the devotees had prepared a two-room apartment.

Prabhupāda stepped through the door and surveyed his sitting room, his eyes widening in appreciation of its simple elegance. It is done in a traditional European style, with molded gilt architraves, walls covered in saffron colored silk wallpaper, and a polished wooden floor covered with a floral patterned carpet.

With satisfaction Prabhupāda told Bhagavān, "Organize this center very nicely. So many people will be happy."

"The devotees are very ecstatic," Bhagavān told him, referring to Prabhupāda's presence.

Śrīla Prabhupāda responded with a humble laugh, "Oh. Yes, there was no hope for my coming. Now I've come, they must be."

The far wall is mainly window, giving Prabhupāda a panoramic view of the countryside. There is a line of large oak trees just opposite, and woods and cornfields stretch away into the distance. Prabhupāda asked Bhagavān if the sun shone through until noon. He was obviously thinking of being able to take his massage in the sunshine while remaining in the privacy of his own room.

"Until five o'clock," Bhagavān said, explaining that there were windows on three sides. When the sun rises it shines through the bedroom, and as it moves across the sky it illumines the sitting room. As Bhagavān showed him through the newly decorated apartment, the devotees' skill and sincere endeavor were everywhere in evidence. Bookshelves and some of the bathroom fittings are made of imported Italian marble, as is the low desk in the sitting room. It is a beautiful pink marble slab with hand carved lotus patterns along the edges resting atop ornamental brass legs. As a final touch the devotees had placed vases of fragrant flowers throughout the rooms.

Sitting behind his desk, beneath a large painting of Śrīla Bhaktisiddhānta Sarasvatī Ṭhākura, Prabhupāda relaxed and voiced his satisfaction with their efforts to serve him. "*Yasya deve parā bhaktir yathā deve tathā gurau/ tasyaite kathitā hy arthāḥ prakāśante mahātmanaḥ.* This desire to serve guru is the qualification. In the spiritual life, this is the secret of success. *Yasya deve parā bhaktir yathā deve tathā gurau.* Our Gaudiya Math people, those who were leaders, they wanted to supersede the order of Guru Mahārāja. Therefore it was failure."

He sat back and admired the room. "Very, very nice." Glancing over the few, but opulent pieces of furniture, he noted that such items are not available in India, or if they are, at a great cost. He asked Bhagavān how many devotees are currently staying in New Māyāpur and was told there are about one hundred and fifty.

"Very good. They are all happy?" Prabhupāda asked.

"Oh, yes," Bhagavān answered.

"Let them come and work little, grow food, eat and chant," he said, and contrasted this pleasant prospect with modern life. "Why should they bother going to the factory, running at five o'clock? Horrible life, horrible civilization. Motor accident, delayed, anxiety, 'Oh, I am delayed, I am delayed.' What is this civilization?"

\* \* \*

Harikeśa Mahārāja brought a few pieces of mail in at about 10:00 a.m. One was from Vāsudeva dāsa in Fiji, also signed by Upendra prabhu. Vāsudeva expressed some concerns about working with a GBC and also about the ownership of the land the temple is being built on. He seemed unclear, despite Śrīla Prabhupāda's last letter stating explicitly the type of management structure he wants there. Prabhupāda was even more specific in his reply this time. "Regarding the situation in Fiji, it is necessary that we come to a proper understanding as to the status of the land and the organization of ISKCON Fiji itself. The first point is that the governing board of ISKCON may have yourself and your brother as members, but must also have the GBC for the zone, Guru Krpa Swami, the GBC Chairman, Tamal Krsna Goswami, and Upendra das as members. The second point is that after ISKCON has been organized in the above way the land which the temple is being constructed on must be leased to ISKCON Fiji with a 99 year unconditional lease with option to renew which I shall approve.

"In case you do not like this arrangement then you may keep the temple as your private property and as my disciple I will give you guidance. But you may not use the ISKCON name to collect funds or to take loans. In this connection until this matter is resolved no loan may be taken from the bank or elsewhere and all collections in the name of ISKCON must stop. If you desire to keep the temple as private property then Upendra das may return to Hawaii and ISKCON Fiji may be dissolved. If you want to consider this project as an ISKCON project then you must abide by the orders and direction of the GBC, which you do not like to do. Now whatever you like let me know."

Prabhupāda also sent a letter to the manager of the bank in Fiji instructing him to wait until he gives him direct authorization before giving out a proposed $80,000 loan to Vāsudeva prabhu. Copies of both letters were sent to Tamal Krishna Goswami, Gurukṛpa Swami, Upendra and Vāsudeva.

From New York, Chāyāvana Swami sent a lengthy letter outlining his previous activities in Africa. He described how the *yātrā*, which consisted of only one temple in Nairobi, was in very poor shape before he took up the management. Devotees were disheartened and in heavy debt, and there were problems with the local government as well as our Hindu supporters. He said he felt Śrīla Prabhupāda had been misinformed about his activities and he requested that the matter be carefully reconsidered, "as I wish to take a responsible and serious role in the management of our Society." He expressed his desire to return to Africa.

Well aware of Chāyāvana's personal problems Prabhupāda wasn't too happy to hear that he wants to leave New York so soon after having arrived there. He replied that Chāyāvana should wait until next year's Māyāpur GBC meetings for a decision.

Yaśodānandana Swami sent a report of his latest preaching programs in Coimbatore in Tamil Nadu, where he met with a prominent *brāhmaṇa* from one of the most strict and orthodox branches of the Madhva-sampradāya, Śrī Subbachar. He first heard of our Movement through reading an article Acyutānanda Swami wrote called *Divya-veṣya*, attacking Māyāvādī philosophy. Favorable to our Movement, Śrī Subbachar endorsed our point of view that a *brāhmaṇa* should be known by quality, not just by birth. Yaśodānandana mentioned how Śrī Subbachar explained that because Mahārāja Priyavrata ruled over the entire earth and deputed his sons to control the nine *varṣas*, it is entirely possible that Americans and Europeans could be descendants of *brāhmaṇa* families. Also he quoted Śrī Subbachar as describing, "Sometimes even though a cow has all the characteristics of a cow (gives milk, four legs etc.) if she does not have the fleshy neck as it is on all the other cows, is this a reason why she should be called a goat? Similarly, if someone has all the qualifications except the birth still he should be accepted as a Brahmin."

Yaśodānandana Mahārāja stated that they have been trying to gain support for the entry of our devotees into the Purī temple, where we are presently not allowed. There is a lot of opposition, mainly, he said, from the *śāktas* who worship Bimalādevī, and from the Purī Śaṅkarācārya, whom he described as a "first-class *asura*." He said he hates our movement and the fact that we wear the *yajña-upavīta*, the sacred thread. Apparently the Puri Śaṅkarācārya is at odds with the Śṛṅgeri Śaṅkarācārya, the latter of whom has given our men a letter of endorsement.

In Prabhupāda's short reply he confirmed Śrī Subbachar's claim. "In regards to your point on the brahmanas being dispersed all over the world, Rsabhadeva's sons were both brahmanas and ksatriyas and were throughout the world. The sons of Nava Yogendra were the brahmanas and another son's progeny were the ksatriyas. So continue this preaching work more and more." He did not comment on the other points in the letter.

Not all of the letters Prabhupāda receives are management affairs. In England he received several gifts and notes of appreciation. He has been given individual donations and offerings here as well. He sent a letter of thanks to Mantrinī dāsī, who gave him one hundred and eight pounds. "I thank you very much for it. Actually you are correct, it is not possible for the disciple to repay the debt to the spiritual master. Therefore the disciple remains eternally indebted to the spiritual master and continually works in such a way that the spiritual master may become pleased upon him for such sincere services rendered. Always follow the four principles, take prasadam, and above all chant your sixteen rounds a day, and thus you will make steady advancement in devotional service. Continue to preach this movement all over the world and thus you will become happy and you will make others happy also."

Bhaktin Odette wrote him a simple heartfelt poem which she gave to him yesterday. "Oh, Father, I can't find words to express myself! Closing my eyes, I can only see the beauty, love and infinite tenderness emanating from your lotus eyes—and in silence I cry out! ... a nostalgic longing ... burning like fire, but, Oh, nearly to be fulfilled ... No, without you ... there is nothing more, and beyond our Lord ... there is no more."

Never negligent of even the simplest service, Prabhupāda encouraged her with a few words, "Please accept my blessings. I am in due receipt of your poem offering and I want to thank you very much for it. I have appreciated the sentiments expressed within and I hope that you will continue to advance more and more in your Krsna consciousness. I hope this meets you in good health. Your ever well-wisher, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami."

\* \* \*

As he took his massage sitting on a straw mat in a patch of sunlight, Prabhupāda glorified the beneficial aspects of sunshine. He told me that in Bengal the tradition is to breastfeed the children for at least six months. They are rubbed with mustard oil and put out in the sun. In this way they become healthy and strong.

## July 30th, 1976

Prabhupāda is still weak, and after a very short morning walk he returned to his quarters without entering the temple room.

He is still full of mucus and alters his diet frequently to speed his recovery. He told me that traditional Indian cooking is such that by proper combination of spices and diet one can cure almost any disease and still enjoy palatable dishes.

Harikeśa Mahārāja is cooking but has not done much of it since leaving Prabhupāda's party in February. Unfortunately he is a little out of practice, and thus far has not quite found the right formula to please His Divine Grace. In fact Prabhupāda is complaining, especially over what he offered him today. Instead of making the usual wet *sabjī* from peas, tomatoes and fried *panīr*, freshly made cheese cubes, Harikeśa decided to cook the *panīr* cubes in a thick sugar solution and make a sweet. When I took the plate into Śrīla Prabhupāda's room from the small kitchen next door, Prabhupāda looked dubiously at the preparation and said, "What is this? Call him immediately." Harikeśa came in a little sheepishly and Śrīla Prabhupāda roundly criticized him for what he called his "mental speculation."

\* \* \*

Prabhupāda sat with Harikeśa Mahārāja and I after his short morning rest. He asked Harikeśa about conditions in the communist countries, telling him that materialistic communism where there is no independent eating, living or thinking is comparable to animal existence, for animals also have no independence. He therefore said we have to try to save everyone by developing centers like this one.

\* \* \*

Again there are problems with a senior devotee. News arrived from Africa via Tamal Krishna Mahārāja that Brahmānanda Swami is having some personal difficulties. Not much detail is known, but Tamal Krishna Mahārāja will investigate further. Brahmānanda Mahārāja is such a senior man that I was a little surprised by Prabhupāda's muted reaction. He shook his head with exasperation and simply told Harikeśa and Bhagavān, "What can I do? The GBC should deal with this."

I remained in the room with Śrīla Prabhupāda after his secretaries had gone out. He became a little contemplative and asked me whether any news had come of Madhudviṣa in Hawaii. I told him that we had heard he is now living with a woman. He showed some surprise and dismay, and then, his features softening in reflectiveness, said, "Sometimes I feel for Madhudviṣa. Also Ṛṣi-kumāra, but by Kṛṣṇa's grace he has returned."

I thought of a morning walk in Hawaii shortly after the news came of Madhudviṣa's leaving, when he had told us that, "You can't cheat guru and Kṛṣṇa, you can only cheat yourself." I asked how it was that apparently advanced devotees fall down. He explained that even good men can fall from their elevated positions because we all have our independence; as soon as this is misused *māyā* is there to punish and reform us. He said that woman means "*māyā*'s weapon," and he noted that even Lord Śiva himself had fallen victim to the Mohinī-mūrti *avatāra* of Lord Kṛṣṇa.

\* \* \*

One of the devotees gave Śrīla Prabhupāda a gold ring with the *mahā-mantra* inscribed on it. He put it on and now wears rings on three fingers of his left hand and two fingers of his right.

\* \* \*

Śrīla Prabhupāda's push to start something in China seems to be bearing fruit. Śrīdhara and Trivikrama Mahārājas sent a report from Hong Kong, where they are now recruiting Chinese devotees. They requested initiation for a young woman who, from their description, seems well-educated and eager to spread Kṛṣṇa consciousness to her fellow countrymen and women.

Śrīla Prabhupāda was pleased to initiate her, and he encouraged his two *sannyāsīs* to go forward with their program. "Yes, I immediately accept for initiation Naisen Wang. Her name shall be Nitya-līlā dāsī and I have personally chanted on her beads which are enclosed. She is a very good devotee and she must immediately be initiated. This girl should be trained up and educated to speak in Chinese and recruit Chinese boys and girls. Just try to create a Chinese group of devotees from Taiwan, then all other things are done automatically. We require immediately a Chinese group of devotees."

Prabhupāda also informed them that Tamal Krishna Mahārāja is arranging to send two men and funds.

## July 31st, 1976

Since we arrived Prabhupāda has been resting until late in the morning, after 7 a.m. He has not taken a full morning walk since leaving New York. This morning he ate very little for breakfast. He also told us to make all endeavor necessary to prevent him from catching cold. He said that, "With an old body, it means thin blood, and this turns to mucus. And when there is too much mucus it blocks the heart, and this is very dangerous." He has spent the last couple of days sitting quietly in his room, but at least he is once again having his massage in the sunshine and taking a full bath.

\* \* \*

Bhūgarbha dāsa, who was with Mahābuddhi dāsa in India heading up the BBT Library Party, came in the afternoon to give a brief report on his activities. Prabhupāda was keen to hear news of distribution of his books in universities and libraries. Bhūgarbha said a professor, Dr. Radhakrishna from the University of Edmonton in Canada, was writing a comparative study of *bhakti* in the Indian and the Hebrew traditions, and he was using Śrīla Prabhupāda's books exclusively as his source for the Indian tradition. The professor had ordered three full sets—one for himself, and two for the university. Bhūgarbha said, "He said, 'What is a good definition of *bhakti*?' So I showed him *The Nectar of Devotion, anyābhilāṣitā-śūnyaṁ jñāna-karmādy-anāvṛtam.* He said that is very good, and he wrote it down and put it in his book."

Prabhupāda nodded. "Till now, they took *bhakti* as a matter of sentiment. Religious science they did not know—all over the world."

"He said he's trying to show that by studying *bhakti* in Indian tradition and also in Hebrew tradition, he's ..."

Prabhupāda cut in. "*Bhakti* is not achieved by studying; *bhakti* stage is achieved by practice. That is the special significance of our institution, that we are engaging our men in practicing. Therefore they are getting knowledge—not by reading."

Bhūgarbha described how the professor's idea was that there are certain social and economic conditions that need to be present before *bhakti* can come about.

"*Bhakti* can solve everything," Prabhupāda said. "Social, economical, cultural, religious, everything."

Bhūgarbha told Prabhupāda that the Library Party was very inspired in Delhi because everywhere they went Śrīla Prabhupāda had already been there himself selling his original three volumes of the *Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam*. "The librarians would remember. We would ask them, 'When did you get these books?' They'd think. 'Well, about ten, twelve years ago, some *sannyāsī* came. We purchased." He said that on the basis of that original purchase they would tell the librarian that they now must complete the set. They would agree, placing standing orders for the remaining volumes.

Prabhupāda said that he had also sold his books to many places in Bombay. Bhūgarbha said they had sold books to the Royal Asiatic Society there. "We had to do a little negotiation with them, but they purchased everything. Then the Calcutta Asiatic Society, they wrote us a letter, they said that, 'These books are the best. But we have no funds to purchase, so can you please send us free of charge?'"

Prabhupāda was a little surprised. "Maybe. Nowadays people are not interested in cultural societies. They are simply for belly; how to earn money, that's all. *‚ūdra* mentality. The *brāhmaṇa* mentality is gone. In America also, people are not joining cultural classes of philosophy. Hayagrīva said he has no job because nobody's taking English as literary study. Nobody's interested, they are taking to technology."

Bhūgarbha confirmed that American professors complained to them. "When we try to sell them personal books, they say that the salary of a college professor in America is the same as the salary of a waiter in some hotel. That is the respect they are given."

Prabhupāda gave a little chuckle. "Sometimes they are called church mouse. A mouse in the church, what he'll eat? He's in a householder's place, a mouse is there, he can eat something. But church, nobody's eating there. Simply dust, that's all."

\* \* \*

There was quite a lot of mail, so while he waited for another meeting, Prabhupāda went over it with Harikeśa.

On June 26th Prabhupāda had inquired from Jayapatāka Swami about Prabhu Swarupa, questioning whether the man was serious about transferring his land in Haridaspur to ISKCON. Jayapatāka's letter today indicated the man was.

Prabhupāda replied, "Let Prabhu Swarup transfer the land immediately, we shall do the needful. You are an intelligent boy so you can take it from me that this Haridaspur scheme is for making a link with Bangaladesh, so we have to deal from that point of view."

Since it was rumored that Prabhu Swarupa was initiated by Bon Mahārāja, Prabhupāda had also questioned his motives. Jayapatāka indicated however, that Prabhu Swarupa was now interested in retaking his initiation from Śrīla Prabhupāda. So Prabhupāda added, "As far as the fresh initiation goes, we shall see later on. I am expecting to receive the land upon arrival."

There was a lengthy letter from Hansadūta Swami, responding to the letter signed by the GBC members in New York. He enclosed with it a copy of a letter he had written to Gopāla Kṛṣṇa prabhu prior to his receipt of the GBC letter. In his letter to Gopāla, Hansadūta denied any intent on his part to want to be involved in the Indian management. "I came to India with a bad taste in my mouth, I did not want to get entangled again in squabbles with Godbrothers resulting in bad feelings and unfounded rumors, as it was the case in Europe." He stressed he had only become a co-GBC of Vṛndāvana because Gopāla himself had insisted on it, and that his actual intent in coming to India was to simply fulfill Śrīla Prabhupāda's desire to create a traveling *saṅkīrtana* party. He told Gopāla that he was becoming a victim of false rumors and was being unduly paranoid about him.

After having received the letter from the GBCs, he now wrote to Śrīla Prabhupāda, "I came to India soley on your divine Graces instruction to start the traveling bus party, which I have done by your mercy alone. At the GBC Meeting I requested my senior Godbrothers from the very beginning that I might be relieved of my zone to be free to preach on the buses in India, and that I did not want to be assigned to a zone, since I could already see so many quarrels going on between Gargamuni Maharaj and Gopal Krishna prabhu."

Because of the difficulties with Gopāla, Hansadūta said he was thinking of taking Haihaya prabhu's advice and buying a private house in Vṛndāvana to serve as his base. In that way he hoped to avoid further problems and continue with his preaching. "For the time being I am staying in Vrindaban, practicing Chaturmasi, and waiting for the buses to return for Janamastami, and also the new buses from Germany to arrive." He ended by assuring Śrīla Prabhupāda that his intention was only to preach, begging his forgiveness for any disturbance he may have caused.

Śrīla Prabhupāda responded to his letter with a solution without getting into the details of who said what, when and to whom, and without recriminations to anyone.
