"You should carry on your sankirtana movement; you are fit for that." When he signed the typed letter later on, he added by hand, "Wherever you like you can make your HQ."

Hṛdayānanda Mahārāja sent good news from the Spanish BBT that the new Spanish *Kṛṣṇa* book was finished and some copies were on their way to Śrīla Prabhupāda in France. He wrote, "I am sure that these books will sell in gigantic quantities in Latin America." He also said they had just sent the *Bhagavad-gītā As It Is* and *Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam* Canto One, Part Two in Portuguese, and four smaller editions of *Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam* in Spanish, to the printer. After a humble prayer begging to be always engaged in Prabhupāda's service, he ended his letter by saying that, "All of the devotees in South America are highly enthusiastic, and only live to read and distribute Your books."

In fact Prabhupāda has already received the copies of the new Spanish *Kṛṣṇa* book and is delighted with them. "With great pleasure I thank you for them. Please offer all the devotees my blessings. Their enthusiasm for distributing my books will please me very much. Not only will I be pleased, but my guru maharaja will also be pleased and they will all be blessed. This is very good news, prithivite ache yato nagaradi grama sarvatra pracara hoibe mora nama, this is the way of preaching, to spread news of Krsna in every town and village all over the world. Thank you very much."

Prabhupāda also received a letter from Paramanand Patel, a twenty-eight year old assistant engineer in Madhya Pradesh in India. Because it was written in Hindi, Śrīla Prabhupāda read it himself and then dictated his reply. Paramanand wrote, "I am in intense grief that my valuable life is uselessly passing away engaged in useless materialistic activities. My intense desire is to devote my whole time in chanting, glorifying and worshiping the Lord." He humbly requested Śrīla Prabhupāda's help to achieve his goal. "Will you give shelter to an ignorant person like me at your lotus feet? I always used to study *Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam* in my childhood. Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa is my *iṣṭa-deva* and He has the highest place in my heart. I beg of you that you please give me shelter in your society and guide me in the path of self-realization. I don't experience any kind of pleasure in the material world."

He said that his parents were arranging for his marriage in about six months, but he was worried that *gṛhastha* life could not be suitable for self-realization. He therefore asked Śrīla Prabhupāda what would be best for him. "I have written my sad story to you. Please guide me to the path of self-realization by which I can completely devote my life in worshiping and glorifying God."

Prabhupāda replied most encouragingly. "By reading your letter, it seems that you are very fortunate. Krsna has given you the best opportunity for developing your Krsna consciousness and certainly He wants to help you. Therefore He has advised you to approach me. As it is the desire of Krsna it is my duty to help you in every respect.

"I shall be very much pleased to see you in person in Bombay and certainly Krsna will give us the opportunity to engage you fully in Krsna conscious service. You are naturally a devotee of Krsna. Pray to Him always for help and chant the maha-mantra; Hare Krishna Hare Krishna Krishna Krishna Hare Hare Hare Rama Hare Rama Rama Rama Hare Hare. Certainly very soon you will get all possible facilities for advancing in Krsna consciousness."

Prabhupāda ended by apologizing for not being able to reply in Hindi due to having no Hindi secretary.

\* \* \*

At about 5:00 p.m. Yogeśvara dāsa and his wife, Jyotirmayī dāsī, who manage the French BBT and *gurukula* respectively, came to discuss the proper standards for the children's schooling. Yogeśvara prabhu just returned from a trip to the printer in Italy, and Prabhupāda asked him what news he had. Yogeśvara reported that the French editons of *Kṛṣṇa* book and *Upadeśāmṛta*, as well as the Italian *Bhagavad-gītā*, will be ready within ten days.

Prabhupāda then suddenly switched topics. "What is the political position of the Fascists and Communists?"

"Very mixed up," Yogeśvara told him.

Bhagavān added with a laugh, "They are called Christian Democrats."

"They can manufacture so many," Prabhupāda said with mild sarcasm. "Fertile brain in the tract of desert world. The fertile land in the desert is called oasis. So similarly these rascals, they have got fertile brain in the world of desert, where there is no happiness. But they have got fertile brain, how to manufacture happiness. And *māyā* kicks on their face and baffles everything. This is the illusion. *Daivī hy eṣā guṇa-mayī mama māyā.* The world is desert, *duḥkhālayam aśāsvatam*, but they have got fertile brain, how to become happy. And as soon as they make some arrangement, kicks on his face and he falls down. That's all."

He glanced over at Harikeśa. With a grin he said, "What do you think? Is it right? Sometimes you have got fertile brain." Then to us all, "If you want to be happy, then you have to go back home, back to Kṛṣṇa. That is the only way. What do you think, Jyotirmayī? You are intelligent."

Jyotirmayī took her cue, not to join in the informal discussion, but to ask her specific questions on the *gurukula.* "Because now, if I don't ask them today ..."

Prabhupāda responded even before she could ask her questions by immediately quoting from the newly released *Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam* Seventh Canto, Part Three. "*Brahmacārī guru-kule vasan dānto guror hitam.* The beginning of life is how to become cent percent obedient to guru. That is *gurukula.* That training should be given. The whole process is that our life will be successful when we strictly follow guru and Kṛṣṇa. Guru means Kṛṣṇa; Kṛṣṇa means guru. Not Māyāvāda, but guru means one who follows Kṛṣṇa, he is guru. *Sākṣād-dharitvena samasta-śāstrair uktas tathā bhāvyata eva sadbhiḥ.* So guru is directly God. *Sākṣād* means directly. So *sākṣād-dharitvena samasta-śāstrair uktas,* in every *śāstra* it is said the guru is one, Kṛṣṇa. So, it is stated in the *śāstra* and it is accepted by authorities. Not that it is simply stated. *Ukta* means 'said,' and *sadbhiḥ,* 'by great personalities,' and *tathā* means 'accordingly.' *Bhāvyata eva sadbhiḥ*, those who are actually in transcendental platform, they should accept it. So why? *Kintu prabhor yaḥ priya eva.* It does not mean Māyāvādī, that he has become God, but he is the most confidential servant. He's God, servant-God; God is master-God. *Kintu prabhor yaḥ priya eva tasya.* So why he has become *priya*? That is, Kṛṣṇa says personally, *na ca tasmān manuṣyeṣu kaścin me priya-kṛttamaḥ:* nobody is dearer than him in the whole world. Why? *Ya idaṁ paramaṁ guhyaṁ mad-bhakteṣu:* 'Who preaches this gospel of *Bhagavad-gītā* among My devotees.'

"So the guru has got two business. He has to make devotees and teach them the principles of *Bhagavad-gītā.* Therefore he's so dear. Because he acts very confidentially on behalf of Kṛṣṇa, therefore he's as good as God. This is *bhakti.* Not the Māyāvādī philosophy that guru has become God. He's servant-God, and Kṛṣṇa is master-God. So the success is that both the Gods, when one is accepted by both the Gods, then his life is success. *Guru-kṛṣṇa-kṛpāya pāya bhakti-latā-bīja.* Therefore one has to fix his faith staunchly in the bona fide guru. So if one has got bona fide guru, and if he follows that bona fide guru, then his life is success. This is the process. So *gurukula* means to teach how to become very, very faithful, cent percent faithful, to the bona fide guru. That is *gurukula.* So you have to teach like that. By behavior, by life, by action. This sum and substance of *gurukula.*"

He was a bit annoyed when he asked for the new edition of the *Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam* and Harikeśa replied we didn't have it. Somewhat caustically Prabhupāda said, "Simply your face, that's all. I'll have to see your face. Why this book is not there?"

I explained that we had only received the two advance copies given to Prabhupāda in New York. We left one behind there, and the other was given to George Harrison.

Telling Harikeśa to see if there was another edition he could look the verses up in, and remarking that "reference book must be always there," Prabhupāda went on with his comments on *gurukula*. "Now from this platform, on this understanding you have to organize."

Jyotirmayī enumerated what she had been telling other teachers were the three main principles children must be taught: obedience, how to read Prabhupāda's books and how to be self-controlled.

Prabhupāda told her that the guru requires four principles: no illicit sex, no meat-eating, no gambling and no intoxication, and chanting at least sixteen rounds of the *mahā-mantra*. "Rise early in the morning, that should be taught. So whatever guru says, you have to teach them perfectly, from childhood; then there will be no deviation when they are grown up."

He stressed that the most important thing is for the children to learn how be obedient, self-controlled and act on behalf of the guru. He said he isn't interested in producing scholars because the world is already full of them. "Put in the life, that is important. Our Movement has drawn the attention of the world on account of life and the knowledge. They are finding the knowledge in the books and they are finding the practical application in the life."

Having found the verses, Harikeśa read out [7.12.1](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-7/12.1) describing the principles of *brahmacārī* life. Prabhupāda then said that the boys and girls should therefore be separated, in order to learn how to control their senses. With a laugh he repeated Sarasvatī, Śyāmasundara and Malatī's daughter, who once said, 'We have no sex with women.' "So, innocent, she does not know. That is, if they are kept separate, they remain innocent."

He said girls should learn how to be faithful to their husbands and like Rādhārāṇī they should learn the sixty-four arts, such as cooking and painting. "Then She could control Kṛṣṇa."

The boys should be taught to address all women as their mother. When they grow up they should learn the *śāstra*. "The more they read, the more they learn, then they become preacher, teacher."

In describing how to organize the school Prabhupāda explained that the system in India is that the older boys teach the younger ones. In this way one teacher can oversee hundreds of students. "Not that everything I have to do. Intelligence is that employ others to help you. Train assistant so that in your absence things can be done. Caitanya Mahāprabhu used to do that. When He was sixteen years old he could argue with Keśava Kāśmīrī because He was practiced. In this way, stage after stage, everyone should be expert. Everyone should be teacher and student."

Bhagavān asked if the boys should learn to cook.

"Huh? I never said that," Prabhupāda said. "Why you are bringing that question? I said the girls should be. Cooking is not boy's business. But cooking is not a very difficult art. If they want, the boys can do. There are so many, in the *Bhakti-rasāmṛta-sindhu* it is stated, how Rādhārāṇī was qualified. So these things should be taught to the girls. If the girls are taught to give service to the husband to the greatest satisfaction, there will be no disagreement."

When Yogeśvara asked if the boys could be trained in a particular service such as press work, Śrīla Prabhupāda was positive. "Oh, yes, everything is devotional. There are varieties. We are not Māyāvādi, impersonalists, finished, all business. It is not like that. So whatever business is going on in our Movement, everything should be taught according to the capacity, boys or girls, it doesn't matter. Some department is suitable for the boys, some department are suitable for the girls. In this way, they should be trained up. But everyone should be trained up to give service. That is *gurukula.*

"And *brahmacārī*, this sex impulse should be controlled. That ruins the whole character. Our big, big *sannyāsīs* are becoming victimized. So that is the danger." He repeated his axiom that women and men are both good, but when they combine they become bad, explaining how sex attraction can be overcome. "In the spiritual world, there is no such combination of sense gratification, therefore it is always good. Everyone is part and parcel of God, so they are good. So you have to train like that. In the spiritual world there are very, very beautiful women, thousand, thousands times, but there is no attraction of sex. They are working together, serving together, everything. But the sex attraction, there is none. They are elevated so much in the service of the Lord. He quoted Yāmunācārya. "When one spits on the sex pleasure, that means he is elevated in spiritual life. So in the material world that is not possible. But by training, by knowledge, one can be elevated. That is *gurukula.* So these are the general principles. Now arrange."

Jyotirmayī said that she was trying to teach the children to live simply; they were not dressing in fancy clothes with jewelry and such things.

Prabhupāda, however, told her, "Don't say 'no.' But give a taste for the good, then it will be automatically 'no.' And if you say 'no' then they will rebel. The four 'no's,' that is very difficult, still they are breaking. No illicit sex, they are breaking. But if they develop Kṛṣṇa consciousness, this will be automatically 'no.' Give them positive life. Then it will be automatically 'no.' And if you say 'no,' that will be a struggle. This is the psychology; positive engagement is devotional service."

He went on to say that it was not meant for everyone, but if a small section of the population was ideal, they could guide human society. "At the present moment, there is no ideal section. Everyone is rascal, demons, rogues, everything. There is no ideal character. All politicians, scientists, leaders, they are all drunkards and woman-hunters. So what they can lead? There is no ideal man in the society. The politicians are giving big, big speech in the United Nations. They'll go to the same hotel where another debauchee is dancing and drinking. That's all. That is his character. Is it not? So what he will do? He can give a very big speech, that's all. What is his character? There is no ideal character in the present human society."

Jyotirmayī also had some questions about the academic side of *gurukula*. She asked if they should teach biology about how the body is working, just to give some general knowledge.

Prabhupāda's response was instantly to say it was a waste of time. He told her that biology is going on, whether you study it or not.

"You were saying they should learn geography and history," Jyotirmayī humbly reminded him, "just for general knowledge."

"That is because you have to go from America to India. You must know." Prabhupāda laughed. "You have to calculate two plus two equal to four, a little mathematics. But this biology and this 'logy,' they are useless. There is no necessity. What you'll gain by understanding biology?"

Then he gave a convincing argument, backed, no doubt, by his many years running a pharmacy. "Even one who knows biology, the medical man, he gives a tablet, 'Perhaps it may help you.' Perhaps. He's not sure. So what is the use? First of all, he'll take one ounce of blood from you, and they send, this station, that station, now making a chart, then he'll give you a tablet, 'Perhaps it may help.' This is going on. Even the biggest pathologist, medical man, cannot guarantee that whatever medicine he gives will work."

In response to a question from Yogeśvara he added that if someone already has medical knowledge then they can be engaged to serve according to what they know. "But not that our men have to go to the medical college to learn medical science. That is not the point."

Jyotirmayī said that since they are living in the country she is already showing the children different plants and explaining their use. In light of what Prabhupāda had just told her, she asked if there was any use in that.

"No," he said. "Different plants, that is botanical study, that has also no utilization. But you can teach them, 'Just see, this plant is coming from earth. The earth is the mother of this plant.' These things you can convince them. Is it not a fact?"

Giving the explanation of how different living beings are born from the earth, he outlined a useful study of plants. "That study will be nice. *Ahaṁ bīja-pradaḥ.* Just like father gives the seed, similarly, Kṛṣṇa gives the seed. The seed, when pushed into the womb of the mother and properly nourished, a rose plant comes out. It is very easy. The father injects the seed within the womb of the mother, and the childs come out. Similarly, whatever is coming out from the earth, the seed-giving father is Kṛṣṇa. This nature's law is going on. Where is the necessity of understanding more than this? We understand the mother is pregnant. Now how she has been, how the child is growing, that is not under your control. It is going on. *Prakṛteḥ kriyamāṇāni guṇaiḥ karmāṇi,* immediately it is in hand of the nature. Even if you study, you cannot understand how things are arranged. The intestine is joined to the navel of the child and the food is supplied, how it is mechanical; do you know everything? Can anyone do? Can anyone understand? But things are there; that is being done by *prakṛti.* Even if you study, you cannot understand. So best thing is to understand that it is being done by nature under the instruction of Supreme Lord. Let us chant Hare Kṛṣṇa instead of studying these. There are many students, many botanists, many ... They, vaguely they are studying, and they have no understanding of Kṛṣṇa. They're denying, rather, the Father. The child has come into existence without father. This is their knowledge. So instead of becoming such a fool and rascal it is better not to study."

To make sure she fully understood Prabhupāda re-emphasized the platform on which he wanted the *gurukula* system to be built. "You follow that, *brahmacārī guru-kule,* that I've already explained. That should be done. Don't bring any new thing, imported ideas. That will not be helpful. It will be encumbrance. 'My experiment with truth'—Gandhi's movement. Truth is truth. Experiment means you do not know what is truth. It is a way of life, everything is stated there. Try to train them, simple thing. We are not going to teach biology or chemistry. Our students are not going to ... Our students should be fit for teaching Kṛṣṇa consciousness, by their character, by their behavior, by their knowledge; that is wanted. Biology, chemists, physicists and mathematician, there are hundreds and thousands. We are not going to waste our time that *gurukula* should produce a great grammarian, a great geologist, biologist; don't want that. There are many other educational institutions. If you can get a good driver of your car, so what is the use of wasting your time to learn driving? Is it not? Better employ one driver, pay him some fare."

Harikeśa recalled Prabhupāda saying once that the big businessmen in India don't bother sending the children to school. "They can make a lot of money by sitting by the phone and just pay a few rupees a day and any educated fool can do the work."

"Yes, they do that," Prabhupāda said. "They are employing in their factory big, big chemist, big, big physicist, engineer and so on, but they do not bother. They are paying thirty thousand rupees per month salary, Birla. Expert, imported from foreign country, but their sons are never troubled. They know how to utilize that worker of thirty thousand rupees per month and to earn thirty *lakhs* from him. Why shall he waste his time? Actually, in order to make a balanced society, the *varṇāśrama-dharma* is very important, cooperation. So these things are meant for the *śūdras,* and *brāhmaṇas* are not meant for this."

Prabhupāda stated that modern man has invented many different occupations simply for earning money, but no one can acquire more than he is destined, therefore life should only be utilized for becoming fully Kṛṣṇa conscious. To confirm this he had Harikeśa read out verse eighteen, Canto One, Chapter Five of the *Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam*. Harikeśa also read the purport in which it was mentioned that higher planets such as the moon have far higher standards of enjoyment than here. That naturally triggered Prabhupāda's criticism of the scientists. "Such a pleasing planet, and these rascals say there is no life. The moon is described everywhere, the most pleasing planet. Actually, when there is moon in the sky, how it is pleasing. So that planet is meant for the high-class pious persons. And they get their life for ten thousands of years, they live very comfortably, drink *soma-rasa.* These are the descriptions we get from *śāstra.* And these rascals say it is desert. And we have to believe these rascal scientists and disregard the description of the *śāstra*. What do you think? Is that very good intelligence?"

We all agreed it wasn't, and he grinned. "We disregard the statement of Vyāsadeva, and we have to accept the statement of a rascal drunkard! We are not so unfortunate. The unfortunate, they can believe that; we cannot believe."

Harikeśa finished the purport, and then Prabhupāda asked Jyotirmayī if she had any final questions.

She did. Noting that Prabhupāda has given Arundhatī permission to teach her own son, she wanted to know if that was a general policy.

Prabhupāda explained, "He complained that, 'My boy is not being properly ... ' So I said, 'You teach your son.'"

"She can keep him and teach him all the time? Until he's older and so on?" Jyotirmayī asked.

"Yes, yes, yes. That is the duty of the father and mother," Prabhupāda assured her. "Along with that, he can teach others also. These things are to be organized. But some way or other, our students should be given education and spiritual life, Kṛṣṇa consciousness. Individually, collectively, somehow or other. The principle is laid down there, *brahmacārī guru-kule vasan dānto guror hitam.* That's the beginning. Everything is there, we have to simply follow it. We haven't got to manufacture anything. That is a waste of time. Whatever is there, you follow. Is that all right?"

Jyotirmayī was satisfied and had no more questions.

Then it was Yogeśvara's turn. He had questions about a preaching opportunity in Thailand. Presenting Śrīla Prabhupāda a parcel of Thai silk, Yogeśvara said that it was a gift from Mr. Jootee Boonsoong, a Thai multimillionaire. The man's former secretary is now a devotee here in France. From her preaching Mr. Boonsoong has taken a strong interest in Kṛṣṇa consciousness, offering now to help establish ISKCON in Thailand. Yogeśvara claimed the man owns one third of all the land in Thailand. He has given us the use of a beautiful house in the center of Bangkok and has invited Yogeśvara prabhu to go there in October to meet with the Prime Minister and has hinted at a possible meeting with the King. Yogeśvara asked Prabhupāda on what level he should present Kṛṣṇa consciousness.

"On the level of *Bhagavad-gītā*," Prabhupāda told him. "God is the supreme controller. And we have to learn how to remain peacefully under the supreme controller, just like citizens and the government. Good citizenship means one who lives under the control of the government. Similarly, a good person is one who is God conscious and lives according to the instruction of God. So there is instruction of God, we are presenting this all over the world."

Yogeśvara wondered how the center would be managed. Prabhupāda told him some men from India could be sent, since it is nearby. He was also confident that local men would soon join. "When there is rice thrown, the crows will come," he said humorously. "If there is no rice, how the crows will come? This is the philosophy. If there is living place then many crows will come."

Prabhupāda wanted to know if Mr. Boonsoong had received any books, and Yogeśvara assured him he had.

Prabhupāda said that formerly Thailand was known as Siam, which means "Śyāma," a name for Kṛṣṇa. "So they are devotees originally," he said. He also mentioned that they manufacture very nice *mūrtis* of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa.

Since Thailand is now predominantly Buddhist, Yogeśvara wondered whether they might object to someone preaching what they may construe to be Hinduism.

"Don't establish Deity," Prabhupāda told him. "Talk on philosophy."

"God is the supreme controller," Yogeśvara repeated.

"Yes," Prabhupāda said. "We accept Lord Buddha as incarnation of God. Show in our books that we have got all respect for Buddha. We do not disrespect Lord Buddha, neither go against him. Anyway, if we get one house to live and a supporter, a big supporter, then our position will be secure. And if our cause is honest, then nobody can check."

Śrīla Prabhupāda also dictated a letter to be sent to Mr. Boonsoong. After first thanking him for his gift and his interest in Kṛṣṇa consciousness he told him, "This Krsna Consciousness Movement is based on the Bhagavad-gita As It Is. We have attempted to present this great philosophy to the world in a pure way, without material motive, and by the grace of Lord Krsna our effort has come out successful. People everywhere are taking to Krsna Consciousness, following the simple principles, and becoming happy. At least no one has ever seen such high character as in our boys and girls. And thoughtful men like yourself are appreciating. Again, my thanks for your consideration."

## August 1st, 1976

Today was Sunday. There were not many visitors because this site is a little remote and as yet not well established.

\* \* \*

Yogeśvara prabhu took some aerial photos of the property at midday. He went off in the morning and returned several hours later as the passenger in a small, single-engined plane. For fifteen minutes he buzzed the Chateau while the devotees gathered in front for his shots. Śrīla Prabhupāda was taking his bath at the time and so wasn't included.

\* \* \*

Having been inside all day and feeling a little stronger, Prabhupāda suddenly decided at about 5:00 p.m. to go for a walk. We hastily got ready, Prabhupāda donning a sweater and scarf before going down to walk around the grounds.

The sun was still shining brightly and the country air warm. About twenty devotees rapidly joined Prabhupāda as he took a short tour. He walked across the grassy fields surrounding the Chateau and along the country lanes. Green and brown fields and lush deciduous forests surrounded us. He inquired about the various crops the devotees are cultivating and was pleased to hear that tomatoes, cauliflower, squash and barley are being grown.

He eventually made his way over to the small cluster of buildings that stand nearby the Chateau. Prabhupāda visited their small cow barn where they have three milking cows and another four will milk soon. The houses the devotees occupy are all built with local stone and the devotees have their own water supply. Prabhupāda went inside one briefly and approved.

Prabhupāda stopped to greet Bhagavān prabhu's wife, Kṛṣṇa-bhāminī, who was holding their toddler, Gauravāṇī, in her arms. She came forward, with Gauravāṇī cautiously holding out a pretty white flower for Prabhupāda. Just as he reached for it, Gauravāṇī suddenly withdrew it and refused to hand it over. Śrīla Prabhupāda laughed like a benevolent grandfather.

On the way back to the Chateau the devotees took him into a large greenhouse where melons, mung *dāl* and a limited variety of flowers are grown. Although the walk was short, it was a real pleasure to see Śrīla Prabhupāda out and about, getting some exercise. He was happy and seemed in his element. He displays a distinct liking for country life, and his enthusiasm for it rubs off on the devotees.

Right afterward he entered the temple room to greet Śrī Śrī Gaura-Nitāi and give a short class, again with the aid of Pṛthu-putra Swami's translation. Speaking on *Bhagavad-gītā* 10.8 he described the real meaning of Kṛṣṇa consciousness. "The Supreme Personality of Godhead is the origin of everything. Everything is emanating from Him. When one understands this fact, he become *budha*, or intelligent. And when one is actually intelligent, *budhā bhāva-samanvitāḥ*, this ecstasy. To come to the spiritual platform, this ecstasy required. So one has to come to the platform of *bhāva,* or ecstasy, gradually."

He described the step by step process of spiritual development as detailed by Śrīla Rūpa Gosvāmī. When he got to describing the stage of *anartha-nivṛtti* he explained how the simple country life he was advocating fitted in with that development. "*Anartha* means unwanted things—they become vanquished. This material world is, means we have created so many unwanted things, this is material world. Just like we are living in this part of your country, a village. So you are living very happily, undoubtedly. There is ample opportunity for living peacefully here. You grow little grains, you get some milk, some vegetable, and all your economic questions solved. But as soon as you go to the city, the whole pollution attacks you. You have to give up this simple eating process. Instead of drinking milk, in the city you'll have to cut throat of the cow and eat the meat. So in this way we shall be implicated with so many sinful activities that our life will be entangled."

He told the devotees that entanglement means having to take another birth in the material world. The materialists, despite their so-called scientific advancement, have no knowledge of this. He explained that a person may get a higher standard of life, but he can also get a lower one. "Just like today I am here. And next life if I get the body of a tree and stand up for five thousand years, is it very nice proposition? In this way we have to understand how the process of life is going on and what is wanted, what is not wanted. In this way, when you are situated, fixed up in your spiritual understanding, that is called *anartha-nivṛttiḥ syāt*, all unwanted things are vanquished.

"So our request is that you live here, very simple life. Kṛṣṇa will supply all your necessities. He's supplying to the birds and beasts, why not to you, devotee? Be confident that you'll get everything, whatever the necessities of life. Live without any sinful activities, don't create unwanted troubles. That is called *anartha-nivṛttiḥ syāt*. So as soon as we are, stop, full stop unwanted things, then *tato niṣṭhā*, then our, that beginning faith becomes firm. That is called *niṣṭhā*. *Tato niṣṭhā tathā rucis*. Then, taste, that one tasted this sort of life, he cannot give up. *Athāsaktiḥ.* Then attachment, then *bhāva*, that *bhāva*. And if we can stay in that *bhāva* stage, then next stage is love of Godhead. And as soon as you come to the standard of love of Godhead, your life is successful. So every instruction is there, books are there, your intelligence is there, and we are trying to give you all possible opportunities. Please stick to this Kṛṣṇa consciousness, and make your life successful."

\* \* \*

The devotees continued chanting ecstatically in the temple, while Śrīla Prabhupāda returned upstairs to his room with some of the leaders. He continued to glorify the country life and expose the shortcomings of the cities. He encouraged them to work hard to propagate his Kṛṣṇa consciousness movement, reminding them of what has already happened here in Europe due to a lack of it. "Organize it and keep hundreds of books. They will live peacefully. But don't entangle in sinful activities. Then it will be all right. Such a nice place, the city residents cannot imagine. What a nonsense life-clubs, slaughterhouse, gambling places, drinking house, this is like hell. Try to save people from this hellish condition of life. Without any knowledge, like animals. And nature therefore creates a wholesale slaughterhouse in war, to cut throat. All finished, many millions and millions. From 1914 to 1950, how many years?"

"Thirty-six," someone answered.

"Within thirty-six years there were two big wars, slaughter. Especially in Europe. Nature will create. Pestilence. Somewhere there is pestilence; somewhere there is war; somewhere there is scarcity of food. But you cannot indulge in sinful activities, then you'll be killed, then nature's law will act. You may defy, that's your business, but nature will act in her own way. *Daivī hy eṣā guṇa-mayī mama māyā duratyayā.* You cannot surpass, that is not possible. But they are foolish, they are trying to conquer over nature by their so-called scientific knowledge. They are such a rascal. You change the color of this fruit and flower, conquer over nature. So rascal, they talk rascal, 'It will take millions of years.' 'We have to wait million?' 'Yes, from chemical we shall bring life, wait million of years.' This is going on."

Referring to his trip to the university campus in Berkeley last year where he saw a big tower from which students had thrown themselves during the turbulent days of the anti-Vietnam war protests, he said, "And for such thing, big building, laboratory, research, scientific research. Big, big signboard. And the students out of disappointment, going to the roof and falling down, committing suicide.

"Very horrible condition. Let them do whatever they like, you live apart from them. Live peacefully in Kṛṣṇa consciousness, be happy. Let these cats and dogs go to hell—what can be done? We are trying to educate them as far as possible, but if they do not take it, that is their business. We are doing our duty, going door to door, 'Read these books. If you like, you can come and live with us.' What we can do more? We do not make any condition that if you live with us you have to fulfill. Of course, the condition is that you should not act sinfully, that is the first condition. But we never say that you have to pay so many dollars. Come. Whatever little food we have got, we shall share.

"So try to understand the importance of this Movement Kṛṣṇa is giving us. This is a first-class place, you can develop it into a Vaikuṇṭha. It is already Vaikuṇṭha, Kṛṣṇa is there, but develop it very nicely, peacefully live, hundreds of miles away from the hellish cities. For little conveyance we can have bullock carts, when we have to get transport. Very peaceful life. Introduce it and live peacefully. Am I right or wrong?"

We all agreed he was completely right.

"These farming projects therefore I introduced: New Vrindaban, it is successful; Philadelphia, it is going on nicely; New Orleans; here also. In London we haven't got much land, but still we have got sufficient land. Everyone is happy, the children, the woman. They don't demand anything, that 'Give us this, give us that.' Automatically they have simplified their life. And gradually develop, make little cottages, grow little vegetable, little barley or wheat and milk. That is sufficient. We don't require much. We don't want luxury, we want just to subsist. *Yāvad-artha-prayojanam.* We hate the idea of luxury, unnecessary. Do the outsider come to see?"

"Yes," Bhagavān said.

"What do they say?" Prabhupāda asked him.

"They are impressed with how much we have done."

"They will be more and more impressed," Prabhupāda affirmed. "What is this city life? In Paris, simply to fulfill the necessities of life, a professional prostitute, so many. And people from all over the world, they come here for indulge in prostitute. From our childhood we know. What a civilization they have made—spoiling the life. Then, after finish this life, you just become a cat, a dog or a tree and stand up. And all other planets are vacant. Simply this planet is filled up; overpopulation—kill them. Why not send there? So vacant land." We were all laughing as Prabhupāda mimicked the scientists. "'That we cannot do.' 'Then what is your scientific research?' 'Yes, we are trying. Wait millions of years.' These bluffing rascals. Don't be misled. Live peacefully here, chant Hare Kṛṣṇa."

As he spoke, Yogeśvara and Guru-gaurāṅga dāsa, the former president of the Geneva temple, were setting up a projector. Now Śrīla Prabhupāda settled back to watch a film of his 1974 European tour in which he was officially honored by the Governor of the Canton of Geneva at the City Hall. There were also shots of Prabhupāda's visit to Paris and of the French devotees out on *saṅkīrtana.* It was only a short clip of a few minutes, but impressive nevertheless. Bhagavān prabhu spoke at the end, "You have done something extraordinary."

Prabhupāda chuckled and summed up his mission. "Therefore I was explaining our ecstasy. Who will feel that ecstasy? That is not possible. They can lecture only—no ecstasy. Here is ecstasy, that is the difference. Ecstasy means immediately on the spiritual platform."

\* \* \*

As he lay quietly on his bed during his evening massage Śrīla Prabhupāda told me that the Americans are the only hope for the world. If the US government can become Kṛṣṇa conscious he said they should immediately finish communism and take control of the whole world. Countries such as in Africa should be controlled by the Americans, he said, for this will be beneficial for them. He described the despotic ruler of Uganda, Idi Amin, as a "gigantic Rākṣasa" who should be captured and publicly killed. Similarly the leaders of any such movement should be dealt with and this will finish their cause. I asked, a little doubtfully, if it was actually possible for any government to become Kṛṣṇa consciousness. "Oh, yes, why not? The people will vote. We simply have to make vigorous propaganda, that's all."

From the comments that Prabhupāda makes it is clear that he is not only thinking how the whole world can be Kṛṣṇa conscious, but that he already has the plan how it can be practically brought about.

## August 2nd, 1976

With no scheduled activity this morning, Prabhupāda relaxed in his room, Harikeśa and I eager to share his time. Although Harikeśa Mahārāja has found direct flights to India, Śrīla Prabhupāda finally decided to accept Atreya Ṛṣi prabhu's invitation to visit Tehran for a few days first.

Prabhupāda said that when he goes to India he would like to travel by car or bus so he can tour all the holy places en route to his specific destination. He said he has always had the desire to do this, but he was too busy, first with family life, then with preaching and writing. He suggested that we arrange for him to travel from one city to another, visiting these sacred *tīrthas* as we go. Although it is a wonderfully enthusiastic hope, none of us is sanguine enough to assume that Prabhupāda will actually be able to stand up to the rigors of such a program. Still, with Śrīla Prabhupāda, we talked with anticipation how it could be arranged.

Prabhupāda began to question Harikeśa about how the communist governments organize themselves. Harikeśa explained that although most people are not Communist party members and they are allowed to vote, the Communist party is the only one allowed, so there is no choice of candidates.

"That doesn't matter," Prabhupāda said optimistically, "the policies we can change. The point is the people have the vote, so we can capture the government."

Harikeśa asked if this was something we could expect to do in the future.

"No, immediately it can be done."

"What? Say in five or ten years?" Harikeśa asked, a little surprised.

"No, immediately," Śrīla Prabhupāda repeated. "They simply have to accept, then immediately. We have to strictly follow the principles in *Bhagavad-gītā*, and then it can be done immediately. But we must follow strictly. How to run economy, how to work—everything is there." As we talked, Prabhupāda at one point described Karl Marx as, "a big Rākṣasa." "I can see by his features," he said.

In this way Prabhupāda enthusiastically discussed the possibilities for preaching in communist countries. Since he was in such a congenial mood, we lingered on, relishing the opportunity to engage in discussion and be educated by Śrīla Prabhupāda's expansive realizations and his vast experience of life. He told us about the different levels of culture in India, explaining that although we don't follow the caste distinctions, still there is a clear difference in the cultural behavior of those coming purely from a high caste family and those from a *śūdra* family.

I observed that there still seem to be many Indians who follow the regulative principles as a matter of social training, although their numbers appear to be waning.

Prabhupāda said that the Bengalis have lost their culture, but in other provinces the *brāhmaṇa* class is still strict. So strict, he said, that no *brāhmaṇa* even accepts food cooked by his own wife, because women are considered equal to the *śūdra* class. They do not even eat food cooked by another *brāhmaṇa*. He said that in Calcutta, where many from the *brāhmaṇa* families accepted service as policemen, the government had to provide special facilities. "They take bath thrice, cook their own food, very strictly. The government had to give them a big hall for cooking. So, it will not take much space, say, little space. One small oven and demarcated: 'This, you see, is mine; and then this is yours, this is yours.' So within that space they'll sit down and cook *dāl, capātīs,* rice, one vegetable, and immediately all the utensils will be cleansed and washed, and the space washed and kept. You'd like to eat, they cook so nicely, although simple. And I have got practical experience: if you cook your own food, whatever it may be, it is healthy."

He contrasted that with life in New York, where people spend so much time commuting to work that they don't have time to eat properly. "Three, four hours to go to work. And again three, four hours to come to home. And work there eight hours. Then what is value? He's shattered. He has no other solace than wine, and he has no other culture. No family-dog friend and television idea—that's all. What his life? Every man has got a dog friend because he has no family. Men, women, and television engagement, I have seen it, all this, in New York."

We discussed how meat-eating was such an integral part of Western society. I described how neither I nor my nephew had a taste for meat as children, but we were forced to accept it until we developed a liking for it.

Prabhupāda told one of his own childhood anecdotes. "When I was one and one-half years old, I suffered from typhoid. And the Dr. Kartika Candra Bose he said that 'Please give him chicken juice.' So my father refused, 'No, no, we cannot.'

"'No, no he has to be given. He has become very weak.'

"'No, no, I cannot allow.'

"'Don't mind, I shall prepare in my own house and send. You simply ...'

"So he took, and my father thought that 'All right, he is doctor.'

"So it was sent from his house. And when it was given to me, immediately I began to vomit. And my father threw it away. And when the doctor asked that this was the ... 'No, no, then don't bother.' This story I heard. This allopathic system of medicine introduced all these things in India. Otherwise they did not know."

Lamenting the horrible condition of modern society, Prabhupāda said, "This meat-eating, chicken juice, tea—these things are unknown to India. No, why India? By nature, you say that you refused meat, although you were born of a father and mother meat-eaters, still. What a horrible civilization they have made. He's human being born, making him animal by culture. Instead of making him more cultured toward the spiritual life, making him redirected again to animal life. This is the Western civilization."

He told us how fortunate our children are, and in doing so revealed his own innocent nature. "Yesterday I was astonished how these children were receiving just like friend, laughing and something saying. You have seen it? As an old friend. Their mother pushes, they would not come. But they were very glad to see me."

My remark that *everyone* was glad to see him did not infringe on Prabhupāda's humble mood. "I was astonished, that how these children take me as friend."

"I don't think that's too difficult. You're the best friend for everyone," I said.

"No, but after all, they are children. How they can take it as it is? So they are fortunate children, and their parents and everyone should take care of them. A very difficult age."

I said, "You always said they're our asset for the future."

"If they can be trained up, they can become very good preacher, each one of them. And they can make hundreds of devotees. In this way we can expand." He looked at us piercingly. "Are you realizing that there is no civilization? Actually civilization we are introducing. Except Āryan civilization, Vedic civilization, there is no civilization-animal society. What do you think? Are you convinced about it?"

Harikeśa had no problem answering. "Oh, yes, every time I walk out the door I'm convinced. And when you come back to the temple, it's marvelous, the spiritual world. No matter what's going on, may be bad, may be good, doesn't matter. It's very relieving."

"Civilization means to push the man forward for perfection. That is civilization," Prabhupāda said. "Society and economic condition, everything should be so arranged that this human child should be gradually pushed for perfection of life, go back home, back to Godhead. This is civilization. And modern civilization is, don't care for what is going to happen. So long you live, eat, drink, be merry, enjoy, that's all-sense gratification. This is called *nāstika-vāda.* Very dangerous. And that is going on all over the world. How a gentleman can live in that society? Therefore my Guru Mahārāja used to say, 'This is not a place for a gentleman.' Formerly, therefore, they used to go away from the society, go in the forest, to give up this bad association. Live alone."

"Practically speaking, that's what we've done," I said. "By your establishing these temples, it's given us some place to go where we can get out of Kali-yuga."

"Therefore our temples should be very carefully managed," Prabhupāda added. "It may not become again another pandemonium. Kṛṣṇa has given us many nice places. People can live very comfortably, there will be no scarcity. Cultivate Kṛṣṇa consciousness very seriously, that is wanted. Therefore in this old age I am struggling so much to see that things are going on nicely. So far I have seen, it is going on nice, but maybe the management is lacking. It may be the *māyā* is very strong, so be careful. All, you are all old students, and try to organize more and more solidly. The children should be taken, you can give lectures to the mothers, that children should be taken care of. They are future hopes. Child is the father of man."

He said that people accuse us of escaping, but in our Society we have all classes of men—*sannyāsī, gṛhastha* and *brahmacārī.* People may think our prohibiting meat-eating is unnatural, but it is not; it is natural.

When Harikeśa observed that the four sinful acts we avoid are all unnatural, Prabhupāda agreed. "Unnatural, yes. What for smoking? What for drinking? How nicely they sit down on the ground and take *prasādam.* Why there is need of table, chair and these dishes and fork and knife and so on, so on? Why?"

"It's hard to cut the meat. You need a good surface," Harikeśa laughed.

Prabhupāda was also laughing. "Our Bon Mahārāja, once I was eating in his festival and ... He's a *baḍa-sāhib.* So he has given fork and knife. So I did not know, I do not remember even which way I took fork. So Bon Mahārāja began to criticize, 'You are going to foreign country you do not know which hand to take this fork and knife?' So I told him, 'I am not going to learn all these things. I am going to teach them something else—to forget it! You went to learn all these things. But I am not going to learn anything.'"

Recalling the rule of the British in India, Prabhupāda said, "Calcutta, oh, it was so nice city, now it is hell. It is the same Calcutta, why is it now hell? People used to say, 'In the British Empire, first London, second Calcutta."

I told him it had just been voted the second dirtiest city in the world.

He asked what was the first.

"Karachi," Harikeśa told him.

Prabhupāda shook his head. "Both of them got *svarāj*, Pakistan and India. Karachi was one of the first-class city. That means after *svarāj* they cannot manage; unfit persons they are on the top of the government."

He reminisced briefly about his young days in Calcutta. His father was not a wealthy man, nor was he poor; he was middle class, with an income of about two hundred and fifty rupees a month, which Prabhupāda calculated was worth about ten times that in modern currency values. Yet his father was able to entertain four or five guests daily, hold festivals and marry off four daughters. "May not be very luxurious life, but there was no scarcity for food and shelter or cloth. Happy. That is wanted, happiness in whatever circumstance. Not that because we did not possess a motorcar, therefore unhappy."

Prabhupāda did actually at one time own a car, a Buick which he bought in 1925. He couldn't drive but on his father's request he had purchased it for eight thousand rupees so that his nephew, who was a good driver, could earn a living using it as a taxi. His father reasoned that at the same time, they could use it for their personal needs. Prabhupāda explained that a part of their culture included caring for widows and their offspring. As one of his sisters was widowed, she came back to her father with her children, where the whole family helped to support them.

Śrīla Prabhupāda moved from sitting behind his desk to sitting on a mat by the windows for his massage in the sunshine. As I rubbed the oil into his smooth skin, and kneaded and squeezed his flesh and muscles, we continued to talk a little more. Prabhupāda summed up the British rule. "On the whole, during British time, people were happy, that I can say. The thing is that Britishers were little afraid that 'If the government is not good, it will go against our credit, that we may agitate.' So they were careful to see that people are happy. But here nobody's careful. Everyone thinks, 'I'm in my own country. Whatever I do, it is all right.' They were conscious, 'We are foreigners. If the management is not good, then it will go against our credit and it will be difficult working such a big Indian empire.' So they were little careful."

I had heard Prabhupāda praise the British rule in the past, and I had also heard him criticize their policies. So for clarification I asked, "Still, due to the British presence, isn't that the main reason why India has become so degraded now? Because they introduced so many bad things?"

"Yes," Prabhupāda concurred. "From cultural point of view, they are degraded. And that was British policy, to kill them culturally. Otherwise not possible to rule over them."

Having been brought up in England I knew the propaganda. "They always advertised that India was so backward, because that was a justification for their being there, that 'We shall go and educate.' Then they could exploit and avoid criticism."

"Yes, so many bad things Britishers introduced," Prabhupāda said. "Bad things means the Western type of civilization."

I said, "Sometimes people, they say, we're always glorifying Indian culture, so why are they so badly off? So we tell them it's because they've given up the culture that they're badly off."

Prabhupāda's gave a "hmm," of assent and closed eyes meditatively, thus bringing our discussion on culture to a close. Harikeśa went off to do his cooking, while I continued with my service of massaging His Divine Grace's transcendental body.

\* \* \*

I made a decision today to reduce my number of rounds. Since arriving in India last year I have been chanting twenty per day, but of late, due to the traveling, that standard has become increasingly difficult to maintain, with the result that the quality has suffered. So I hope by going back to sixteen I will have a little more time to hear them properly instead of being in anxiety to complete them.

\* \* \*

About twenty-five or thirty *gurukula* children and some of their parents had a special half hour *darśana* with Prabhupāda in his room this afternoon. One by one the children filed in to offer their *daṇḍavats* in front of his desk. They then settled in a semicircle, facing him, on the opposite side of the room. He had them chant the *mahā-mantra* loudly for about fifteen minutes. It wasn't singing and it wasn't *japa*, but a rythmic chant in unison that grew in pace and volume. They began to clap in time, getting caught up in a swell of enthusiasm for Kṛṣṇa's holy name and His pure devotee. The bright faced children were eager to reciprocate Prabhupāda's smiles of encouragement, and Prabhupāda's pleasure at seeing their innocence and purity being nurtured by the lifestyle he has given them was clear to all.

Prabhupāda distributed cookies to them. Then he commented that anyone, simply by voluntarily offering obeisances, "immediately becomes fifty per cent advanced."

Although most of the children were no more than five or six years old, he had no hesitation in speaking the timeless philosophy of Kṛṣṇa consciousness. Quoting from *Bhagavad-gītā* [18.66](https://vedarama.com/en/books/bg/18.66) he said devotional service begins with surrender. But he said the material disease is that everyone wants to become master; nobody wants to become a servant. Therefore there is a struggle for existence.

He said the history of Europe is one of war—one leader after another trying to become the master. The "mastership competition" is going on life after life and in different species of life, but it is a false ambition. "And at the time of death, when this body finishes, the mind absorbed in that mastership idea takes me to another body according to my ambition. So I become again manifest in different body to exhibit my mastership, another chapter begins. So they do not know how these subtle laws of material nature is working to give us opportunity to become master according to our idea, false idea. And we are actually suffering, sometimes as human being, sometimes as animal, sometimes as trees, sometimes as dog. So mastership cannot be attained, that is not possible. In the false idea to become master, we are becoming slaves of the laws of material nature."

However, if by chance, after many births, a person gets association with a servant of the Lord, then he can understand he is not the master, but a servant of Kṛṣṇa. Then he surrenders. He explained that such a person is a great soul and is very rare. "This is the beginning, *man-manā bhava mad-bhakto mad-yājī māṁ namaskuru*. *Namaskuru* means 'Just offer your obeisances unto Me.' So in the absence of Kṛṣṇa—He is everywhere, but He sends His representative. So if we begin, offer *namaskuru* to the representative, it goes to Kṛṣṇa. And then gradually by the grace of Kṛṣṇa one becomes Kṛṣṇa conscious and becomes situated in his own original consciousness, Kṛṣṇa consciousness, and that is the perfection of life."

Among the group was Malatī dāsī, one of the original San Francisco devotees and a member of the original team of six that Śrīla Prabhupāda sent to London to begin things there. She had her daughter Sarasvatī with her, whose example Prabhupāda so often cites as an illustration of how simple it is to preach. Prabhupāda was pleased to see her, and as the meeting came to a close and the other devotees filed out, he called her over and asked how things were. Malatī is preaching in Amsterdam, selling books in both Holland and Belgium. She reported that the center there is preparing to install Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa Deities on September 1st, and on *saṅkīrtana* they are selling about fifteen hundred *Bhagavad-gītā*s per week.

Another devotee he recognized was Annadā dāsī, the daughter of an Indian overseas diplomat, and Bhūgarbha dāsa's wife. Śrīla Prabhupāda complimented her husband as a good preacher and book distributor, and her for her earlier attempts to distribute his books. He told her, "So preaching is our life. The more we preach, the more we are successful. *Yāre dekha tāre kaha kṛṣṇa-upadeśa.* This is Caitanya Mahāprabhu's preaching. Every one of you become guru and deliver the residents of your neighborhood. How to become guru? It is not difficult. What Kṛṣṇa has said, instruct them. You simply repeat it, that's all."

Quoting Kṛṣṇa's request that one always think of Him, become His devotee, bow down before Him, and always worship Him, Prabhupāda said that by inducing just one person to do these four things, one becomes a guru. By merely attempting to inform people of this message, a person is recognized by Kṛṣṇa. "Just like a canvasser, salesman, goes to the market, tries his best to secure some business. The master sees the report how he has worked. Even though he has not secured a single *paisa* business, but he has tried to introduce the goods, then he's bona fide. Similarly, we have to simply carry the message of Kṛṣṇa and try to convince people. If one is convinced, it is good, if not, doesn't matter. Then you are recognized by Kṛṣṇa. Recognition means you become the dearest servant of Kṛṣṇa. Then what do you want more? If Kṛṣṇa recognizes that 'You are My most dear servant,' then what do you want more? So this message was to be carried by all Indians. That is Caitanya Mahāprabhu's desire."

\* \* \*

At 6:15 p.m. Śrīla Prabhupāda went out for a walk, this time to tour the whole property. A group of about thirty devotees were already waiting for him at the foot of the wide stone staircase that forms the main entrance to the Chateau. Walking steadily in the bright evening sun, Bhagavān prabhu took Prabhupāda around the grounds and then to the east of the property to a large factory building nearby. It is being rented from the owner, who used it to manufacture boats and plastics. The devotees now operate Spiritual Sky incense company from it. Sales extend through France, Germany, Holland and Belgium, and last year the business gave $80,000 to the temple.

Prabhupāda was pleased to see everything and inquired where they obtained the ingredients of their various products from. He then suggested that they could make toothpaste from his original formula. "Actually I could give hundreds of formulas," he said, "enough to start a big factory. But I do not wish to divert their attention."

Walking back up the gently rising driveway toward the Chateau, Prabhupāda became a little fatigued. Looking over to a large tree he decided to sit for a while beneath its spreading branches. It was warm enough for him to remove his sweater, and as he sat on the grass on a blanket provided by the devotees, we all sat surrounding him. Bhagavān prabhu played *mṛdaṅga* and led a *kīrtana* with his sweet and melodic voice. Prabhupāda clapped and encouraged the children to do so also. It was an unexpected bonus for us all, and everyone was very happy to sit so informally participating in *kīrtana* with their spiritual master.

The chanting ended and Prabhupāda decided to speak for a few minutes, reflecting on the sweet mood of the occasion. He described the process of *bhakti* as the only way by which the self can be truly satisfied. "*Yato bhaktir adhokṣaje*. How to become engaged in the service of the Lord, that is religion. And this service of the Lord cannot be checked. *Ahaituky apratihatā*. It is not that for certain reason one has to engage himself in devotional service. It is spontaneous. And *apratihatā*, without any check. Just like we are sitting down here—there is no check, anywhere we can sit down. It is not conditional; you can perform service, *kīrtana*, without any check. Not that we have to live in that palace, then we can chant. No. We can live, we can sit down underneath a tree and chant. There is no limit, we can go on. So we have to adjust things in such a way that without any condition, without any check, we can go on with our devotional service.

"Here is the opportunity, this land is very good. You can sit down anywhere and chant this Hare Kṛṣṇa *mahā-mantra*. There is no need of chair or cushion or anything else. And *yenātmā suprasīdati*, that will please your everything, your heart, your mind, your body, your soul-everything. This is the easiest method for achieving the highest perfection of life. So go on with this process without any check, and be happy."

Some devotees had brought over a palanquin, and to the strains of another blissful *kīrtana*, they happily carried Śrīla Prabhupāda back to the Chateau and up the stairs into the entrance.

\* \* \*

Once again comfortably ensconced in his room, Prabhupāda relaxed on his *āsana*, reflecting on how peaceful country life is. "In the city you go, thousands of cars are running, *ror-ror-ror-ror-ror-ror-ror.* What is called? Flyway, expressway, downway, every ten yards stop for the light—how artificial life. And with all these things, if people would have been happy, all right. But they're not happy, in spite of all this advancement."

As the outdoor session had been exceptionally blissful, I enthused a little about it. "It was so nice sitting underneath the tree there, chanting. I was thinking, this is what we could do forever, twenty-four hours. No need to do anything else."

Prabhupāda tipped his head slightly to the side in agreement. "Prospective place, this. Very future prospect."

"Maybe now we don't have so many devotees for all these big places we're buying," I said. "But even just in five years or ten years they'll be full; we'll have to expand more and more. Your idea for fifty percent for books, fifty percent for buildings is very wonderful. In *Caitanya-caritāmṛta* you said that the book distribution and the establishment of temples should go in parallel lines, side by side."

"Going on, up to date, to my satisfaction it is going on," Prabhupāda confirmed.

I responded then that if he was satisfied, we could know that everything will be successful.

But Prabhupāda tempered his positive outlook with a cautionary note. "Yes, but they fight amongst themselves, the GBCs."

Harikeśa entered, bearing gifts given by one of the devotees, Rādhe Śyāma dāsa. He showed Śrīla Prabhupāda some bottles of nutmeg oil, and a massage oil which included menthol, peppermint, eucalyptol, menthol salicilate and oil of lavender in its ingredients. Prabhupāda looked at them but made no suggestion that he would prefer them to his usual mustard oil. Harikeśa said the oils were purchased from a big Buddhist temple in Malayasia, and he then informed Prabhupāda that a big temple in Kuala Lumpar that Prabhupāda had laid the cornerstone for about four years ago, was now completed at a cost of one million dollars. Harikeśa said the man who built it wants to give it to Prabhupāda.

When I showed him another gift from Penang, Prabhupāda reminisced about his stay there at the house of an Indian gentleman. "His wife made very nice *kachaurī*," he said smiling. "They asked, 'What you want to eat?' 'If you can, you make first-class *kachaurī*.' That is from my childhood. My friends also did it. They'd make the first-class *kachaurīs* in my youthhood. I am fond of *kachaurī. Kachaurī* is made first-class in Agra and Mathurā. Very, very nice. The *kachaurī* is being made, hundreds of customers waiting. At shops, there was many shops, waiting for purchasing. And as soon as it comes out of the pan, immediately sold, there is no question of waiting. They make spice nicest. That is India's craftmanship."

He said that there was no question of starvation for want of money. Anyone could sit down and cook something palatable; people would purchase it. "So your livelihood will go on. *Pakorā, kachaurī, jalebī,* anything—people are fond of eating some palatable things, that is their hobby. In Allahabad, there was a *brāhmaṇa.* I had my business, and he was neighborhood, he was living. So in the morning the husband and wife would go to take bath in the Ganges. They would very nicely take bath, and while coming they will purchase some ingredients and then come home. The husband will perform *pūjā,* and the wife will prepare many nice preparations—*baḍa, pakorā,* this, that. Then he'll take his meals, rest awhile, and in the evening he will sit down, he was sitting just in front of my shop, about four or five o'clock with all the preparations his wife had made whole day. And the university students will come up to night, ten o'clock, he'll finish. Nothing will remain. And he'll make at least ten rupees profit, minimum. In those days, 1925, in those days ten rupees means nowadays at least fifty rupees. So, and living very happy. Living humbly as a *brāhmaṇa*. Very prosperous. Living peacefully, husband and wife. There are many such families. If wife is very good, then his home is very nice. They cannot be unhappy at any circumstances. *Dampatyoḥ kalaho nāsti tatra śrīḥ svayam āgatāḥ*—Cāṇakya Paṇḍita. When there is full agreement between husband and wife, cooperation, then the goddess of fortune comes there without application. You haven't got to ask goddess of fortune, 'Please come and help me.' She'll come automatically. This is Cāṇakya Paṇḍita's instruction."

Once more he glorified India's culture. "There are so many things in Indian culture for becoming happy and advancing toward the goal of life. Now I am appreciating more and more, seeing the whole world, what is India's culture. Formerly I was thinking, 'It is custom. To become faithful wife, this is custom.' But when I come outside I see what is wife, and what is faithful wife. In India still, in the village, even there is fight between husband, the wife is faithful. Still. Completely dependent on husband. The husband also, in spite of fighting is always careful that the wife does not get any inconvenience. It was the culture, now it is breaking. In material world for peaceful life there must be peaceful condition between the husband and wife. Everyone requires wife, everyone requires husband. Sex is necessary, so make the condition of sex very peaceful. Why disturbed? As eating is necessary, sleeping is necessary, for ordinary man, so sex is also necessary. So make a condition so that nothing will be disturbed; and in undisturbed condition of mind execute spiritual advancement. This is Indian civilization, aim is spiritual advancement. And to make condition favorable, there are so many things. Here in the Western countries there is no favorable condition. First of all, they have no idea of spiritual life, the goal of life, neither there is favorable condition. And gradually things are becoming degrading. On my last tour in Chicago I saw. In three weeks she has twice divorced, one lady's advertised."

Speaking of eating, Harikeśa, who still hasn't managed to get Prabhupāda's cooking quite right, asked how he found today's lunch.

Śrīla Prabhupāda's comments amazed me with his attention to detail. "The potatoes and *karelā* should be fried."

"Yes, it was fried. I fried it with the cover on," Harikeśa assured him.

"No, not in the beginning. Fry it, and if it is still hard, then ..."

"Then put the cover on. Oh, all right."

"Yes, not from beginning."

"Oh, I made a mistake," Harikeśa understood.

"If you cover from the beginning, the water which is already there will be coming out. And the idea is the water should be taken away. Then it will be tasteful. Still, it was good."

Harikeśa has been a bit feverish today and he asked Śrīla Prabhupāda if he should cook tomorrow if he still has a fever. He was concerned that his sickness might affect Śrīla Prabhupāda. But Prabhupāda was concerned about Harikeśa's health. He told him that if he is sick, there are so many others who can cook for him.

Harikeśa, who seems to have been ill since we were in India together at the beginning of this year, lamented that he could not tolerate being sick any more.

Prabhupāda shrugged. "The body means sickness; the body itself is sickness."

Harikeśa laughed. He said that in illusion he had returned from India thinking he would get well, but he was sick here in the West also. He noted though that Śrīla Prabhupāda seemed to be getting much better.

Prabhupāda confirmed that he was a little better.

Harikeśa went out and Prabhupāda sent for Bhagavān prabhu to discuss the project here. When he came he told him, "I am thinking of how to utilize the whole land. The situation is very good, good prospect. I want that self—independent here, as far as possible. But you have got enough materials. With woods you can make cottages. Then land becomes clear, then utilize it. Give facility to people. Here is very nice arrangement, now make a plan how to utilize. You have enough land, you can utilize for supplying the necessities of life."

Bhagavān agreed it was a wonderful place.

"Yes," Prabhupāda said. "We can get many wonderful places like this all over the world, but they have not been taught how to utilize them."

Bhagavān told Prabhupāda how enlivened the devotees were sitting under the tree with him tonight.

Prabhupāda laughed. He said that was his tendency from childhood. His grandmother kept a roof garden, and all the grandchildren helped her with it. "So we took very much pleasure in watering. But my special tendency was that along with the plants, I, with the bushes, I'll sit down. My tendency. And I'll sit down for hours. And like that, in my childhood. In my maternal uncle's house also, I was doing that. As soon as I find some bush, I make a sitting place."

He said that actually this kind of life is not meant for everybody, only for those who are fortunate. He quoted the verse from *Śrī Caitanya-caritāmṛta* which describes how if one is fortunate he can obtain the mercy of guru and Kṛṣṇa, and thus receive the seed of *bhakti*. It was an appropriate analogy, and he had me read aloud the section which describes the watering and growth of that seed.

Bhagavān had a question about the cows. He wanted to know what the system was for separating the calves because sometimes the cows cry for their young.

Prabhupāda explained that the cow's milk for the first week after the birth of the calf was not fit for human consumption, so at that time the calf is allowed to remain, provided they don't drink too much. After that, the process is to bring the young calves in only at milking time, once or twice a day. This causes the mothers to produce more because they become happy to see their offspring.

"Of course, we are born in big, big towns, we do not know," Prabhupāda said modestly. "But I know this is the process. In Allahabad I was keeping cow, there was facility."

Once again I found myself completely impressed by his humility. Despite his saying, "we do not know," to me it seems that there is no question that Śrīla Prabhupāda cannot satisfactorily answer.

\* \* \*

Late in the evening, about 9:30 p.m. Bhagavān brought an English couple, Haribolānanda dāsa and his wife, to Prabhupāda's room. They carried in a large basket of vegetables and fruits they had grown, to show Prabhupāda. There were marrows, zucchinis, peas, beans, potatoes, tomatoes, pears, apples, lemon spinach, chickpeas and a variety of flowers.

Prabhupāda became so enthusiastic to see their produce that he instructed me to immediately cook the peas and mix them with chilis and dry roasted puffed rice. When I showed some surprise that he was going to eat so late, he laughed it off. He took the snack before resting, enjoying it greatly. He also called for Mandakini dāsī and asked her to make *kachaurīs* with the peas, for his breakfast.

When I asked him if they should be hot, he replied with a grin, "*Kachaurī means* hot."

\* \* \*

Prabhupāda retired at 10:30 p.m. and I massaged him until ten minutes after midnight, the longest session since we left Māyāpur.

As he lay in the half-light, I mentioned that I had heard some of the temples were using frozen foods for their Deity offerings.

Prabhupāda shook his head and gave a sour look. "Tamasic food, tamasic activities! It is going on simply by Kṛṣṇa's mercy!"

## August 3rd, 1976

Jayatīrtha prabhu reported today that there are some new problems in Germany. Hansadūta Mahārāja's recent visit to gather men and equipment for his Indian preaching program generated a good deal of conflict. His men are just about to join him in India but apparently they are helping themselves to vehicles, equipment and money, despite the protests of the temple managers and Jayatīrtha prabhu, the GBC.

After meeting with Jayatīrtha, Bhagavān and Harikeśa, Śrīla Prabhupāda agreed to their proposal to call Hansadūta's men here to France so that he can personally meet with them.

\* \* \*

With little other scheduled activity Śrīla Prabhupāda is holding lengthy conversations, mainly with Bhagavān and Harikeśa, on a range of subjects. I have been able to sit in on them also. Around 5:00 p.m. he was discussing the problem in India of frequent accusations that we are a front for the CIA. This idea is taken seriously enough that it has been raised in Parliament, and Prabhupāda has repeatedly ridiculed their paranoia. Today he laughed and poked fun at their foolishness. "The whole world is becoming CIA! We can say that, 'All right, the Americans have sent their CIA; but why the Germans business there? They are also CIA?' Soon the Russians also will join, the Polish also will join, everyone will join."

"They can't say the Russians are CIA," Harikeśa laughed.

"No," Śrīla Prabhupāda agreed. "We have got potency to force everyone to join. The Russians have already imperceptibly joined—they have praised my books. That is imperceptible, what is called?"

"*Ajñāta-sukṛti,*" Harikeśa suggested.

"Ah. In East Germany also, they have placed order, so this is joining. Just like for us, if you bring any other literature, we throw it away immediately; we take it as useless. Actually it is. We have nothing to learn from them, anything. All bogus. Either he's scientist or astronomer, or ..., we know they are talking all bogus things. There may be some truth. Even when a child speaks, there is some truth. When a child speaks to his parents, there is some truth, otherwise where is the question of talking? So little portion truth is there, everywhere. But when they talk of big, big things—they are going to Mars and scratching sand there—that we don't believe. When they talk of this tape recorder, some electronic machine, joining together and it is working, that much care you can take. But when you speak of so many things, that millions of years there were germs and germination, now they are trying to come out, and it is all vacant—these are all bogus, we don't accept. Talking too much. In Bengal it is called *yatam*. When the child speaks something too much, 'Ah, stop.' To the extent of his capacity, that's all right; but if you talk more than that, then you are rascal. So they are doing that now. Because they have got some electronic success, or they have manufactured some jet plane, they are now thinking, 'Now we have owned over the whole world situation.' That is nonsense. That is *yatam*, speaking more than their capacity. And so far we are concerned, we don't talk anything, except what is mentioned in the books. That's all. We remain always foolish. And as foolish men, we do not talk. We simply talk what is mentioned by Vyāsadeva, by Śukadeva Gosvāmī."

As he spoke, the screams and shouts of children on the grounds below pierced the quiet, causing him to stop momentarily. Bhagavān had to shout down to have them move away. Prabhupāda has often commented that the sex impulse is so strong that people willingly accept the great consequential burden of raising children rather than give it up, and this incident elicited furthur observations from him. He said that sex is the trap of *māyā*, the means by which she captivates all the living entities in the material world, but actually it is merely the pleasure of itching. "Everyone knows it, that 'I may enjoy sex pleasure now; the aftereffect will be very bad.' *Bahu-duḥkha-bhājaḥ.* But why people do it again and again? *Tṛpyanti neha kṛpaṇā.* Those who are *kṛpaṇa-kṛpaṇa* means not *brāhmaṇa—*those who are not trained up as a *brāhmaṇa,* they cannot tolerate this itching sensation. They become victimized, and the aftereffect is very, very bad, either illicit or not illicit. They know it, the modern civilization, they have adopted the means of killing. First of all they try to stop pregnancy by contraceptive method, and still if it is not stopped, then kill. And if he's still born, then again they put up in a box and go away. You know this?"

Harikeśa Mahārāja knew exactly what he was referring to. "Yes, the baby, they put it in a closet and lock the door and walk out."

Prabhupāda was thinking of something Trivikrama Mahārāja had told him in Hawaii about abandoned babies in the airport lockers in Japan. "They put, and when the obnoxious smell comes, they open it and they find. Mother has become so kind. They put in a box and lock it up.

"These are happening. But when you talk of that, 'You learn how to become *brahmacārī,*' that they will refuse. This is the position. The aftereffect is very, very bad, either you get legally or illegally. Legally, we have to raise the children very nicely. Otherwise, they will, unwanted children, create so much trouble. You have to take care for their proper education, of their clothes. We say, 'Nevermind. You have got children—give them proper education, make them devotees, make their life successful.' We cannot say that 'You kill them.' That we cannot say; that is not possible. We welcome. But we must be well organized to utilize these poor souls for becoming first-class devotees. That should be done. Otherwise, sex life and the by-product, that is always troublesome; either you take this way or that way, it is troublesome. If it is not troublesome, why they are killing their own children? To avoid trouble. This is psychology, they want to avoid trouble. But our process is, if you want to avoid trouble, then don't marry, remain *brahmacārī.* If you cannot, then all right, have legal wife, get children and raise them very nicely, make them Vaiṣṇavas, take the responsibility.

"So we are organizing this Society, we welcome. Some way or other we shall arrange for shelter. But to take care of the children, to educate them, that will depend on their parents. Now our Pradyumna was complaining that in the *gurukula* his child was not educated to count one, two, three, four. So I have told him that 'You educate your child. Let the mother educate in English and you educate him in Sanskrit.' So similarly every father, mother should take care that in future they may not be a batch of unwanted children. We can welcome hundreds and thousands of children. There is no question of economic problem, we know that. But the father, mother must take care at least."

He repeated what he had told Jyotirmayī the other day, that the children should be trained from the very beginning how to be devotees. "They should be trained up how to take bath, how to chant Hare Kṛṣṇa or some Vedic *mantra*, go to the temple, offer obeisances, prayer, then take their lunch.... In this way, they should be always engaged, then they'll be trained up. Simple thing. We don't want to train them as big grammarians. No, that is not wanted.
